question: What does the 'cascade' in Cascading Style Sheets mean, and how is it different from inheritance?
model_answer: The cascade is the algorithm the browser uses to resolve conflicting rules, that is, several declarations setting the same property on the same element. It compares them in order: origin and importance (browser defaults, author styles, !important), inline style attributes, cascade layers, specificity, and finally source order, where the later rule wins. Inheritance is a separate mechanism: when an element has no declared value for an inherited property, it takes the computed value from its parent element. Text-related properties such as color, font-family and line-height are inherited properties; box properties such as margin, padding, border and background are not. The keywords inherit, initial and unset control this explicitly.

question: Explain the difference between the selectors `div p`, `div > p`, `div + p` and `div ~ p`.
model_answer: `div p` uses the descendant combinator: it matches every p nested anywhere inside a div, at any depth. `div > p` uses the child combinator: it matches only p elements that are direct children of a div. `div + p` uses the adjacent sibling combinator: it matches a p only when it comes immediately after a div and both share the same parent. `div ~ p` uses the general sibling combinator: it matches every p that follows a div with the same parent, not just the next one. Sibling combinators only look forward in the document, never at earlier siblings.

model_answer:
Specificity is written as (IDs, classes/attributes/pseudo-classes, type selectors) and compared column by column from the left.

- `:where(#main) a.link.active` = (0,2,1), because :where() always adds zero specificity
All four selectors match the link. The two selectors containing an ID win the first column, because an ID beats any number of classes; between them, (1,1,1) has more classes, so the link is purple. Source order is only used when specificity is exactly equal.

question: A developer adds `.btn-primary { background: green; }` at the end of the stylesheet, but the button inside the header stays blue because of an earlier rule `#header .nav button { background: blue; }`. Why doesn't the later rule win, and how would you fix it without using !important?
model_answer:
Source order only decides between rules of equal specificity. `#header .nav button` has specificity (1,1,1) while `.btn-primary` is only (0,1,0), and an ID outweighs classes, so the earlier rule wins wherever it matches.

Fixes, best first:
1. Lower the specificity of the old rule: style with classes instead of IDs, e.g. `.nav-button { background: blue; }`, and keep selectors flat with a naming convention such as BEM.
2. If the old rule comes from a library you cannot edit, load it into a lower cascade layer (`@layer vendor, app;`) so your later-layer rules win regardless of specificity, or wrap its selectors in `:where()` to give them zero specificity.
3. As a short-term patch, match or exceed its weight: `#header .nav .btn-primary` = (1,2,0).
Avoid !important: it can only be beaten by another !important and escalates into a specificity war.

question: What is the CSS box model?
model_answer: The box model describes how every element is rendered as a rectangular box made of four layers, from the inside out. The content area holds text or child elements and is sized by width and height. Padding is the space between the content and the border, and it shows the element's background. The border wraps the padding. Margin is the transparent space outside the border that separates the element from its neighbours. Whether width and height include padding and border is controlled by the box-sizing property.

question: An element has `width: 300px; padding: 20px; border: 5px solid;`. What is its rendered width with `box-sizing: content-box` and with `box-sizing: border-box`, and why do most projects apply border-box globally?
model_answer: With content-box, the default, width sets only the content area, so padding and border are added on top: 300 + 2 x 20 + 2 x 5 = 350px. Teams add a global reset, `*, *::before, *::after { box-sizing: border-box; }`, because sizing becomes predictable: a column with `width: 50%` and padding still takes exactly half the space instead of overflowing.

question: What is the difference between `display: block`, `display: inline` and `display: inline-block`? Why does setting width and height on a `<span>` do nothing?
model_answer: A block element starts on a new line and stretches to the full width of its container by default; it respects width, height, padding and margin on all sides (div, p, h1). An inline element sits on the same line as surrounding text and is only as wide as its content; width and height are ignored and vertical margins do not push other lines away (span, a, strong). An inline-block element flows on the same line like inline, but its box respects width, height and vertical padding and margins like a block, which suits buttons or badges. A span is inline by default, so width and height are ignored until you change it to inline-block or block.

question: Your site scrolls sideways on mobile phones even though it looks fine on a laptop. How would you track down the element causing it, and what are the usual causes and fixes?
model_answer:
To find it, open DevTools device mode, scroll right to see what sticks out, and temporarily add `* { outline: 1px solid red; }` to see which box crosses the viewport edge; hiding elements one at a time also narrows it down.

Usual causes and fixes:
- A fixed width or min-width in px wider than the screen: use max-width, percentages or flexible flex/grid tracks.
- Images or videos with no size limit: `img, video { max-width: 100%; height: auto; }`.
- `width: 100%` plus padding under content-box: use `box-sizing: border-box`.
- Sections set to `width: 100vw`: vw includes the vertical scrollbar, so on browsers with classic scrollbars the section is wider than the page; use width: 100% instead.
- Long unbroken text such as URLs: `overflow-wrap: anywhere;`.
- Wide tables or code blocks: wrap them in a container with `overflow-x: auto;`.
- Elements pushed out by negative margins or absolute positioning.
Avoid just adding `overflow-x: hidden` to a wrapper: it hides the symptom, can cut off content and turns the wrapper into a scroll container, which breaks position: sticky.

question: Explain the CSS `position` values static, relative, absolute, fixed and sticky. What is an absolutely positioned element positioned relative to?
model_answer: static is the default: the element stays in normal flow and top/left offsets and z-index have no effect. relative keeps the element in normal flow, reserving its original space, but shifts it visually by its top/left offsets; it is often used just to make the element the containing block for absolute children. absolute removes the element from flow (no space is reserved) and places it relative to its nearest positioned ancestor, meaning the closest ancestor whose position is not static, or the initial containing block if there is none. fixed also removes the element from flow and positions it relative to the viewport, so it stays put while scrolling (unless an ancestor has a transform). sticky behaves like relative until the scroll position reaches its threshold, such as top: 0, and then sticks within its parent.
keywords: normal flow, original space, top/left offsets, nearest positioned ancestor, removed from flow, viewport, scroll threshold, containing block
expected_answer_points: static: default, normal flow, offsets have no effect | relative: stays in flow, shifted visually, becomes a containing block | absolute: out of flow, positioned against the nearest positioned ancestor | fixed: out of flow, positioned against the viewport | sticky: acts relative until a scroll threshold, then sticks inside its parent
common_mistakes: Saying absolute is relative to the direct parent even when that parent is not positioned | Thinking relative removes the element from normal flow | Forgetting that sticky needs a threshold such as top: 0

Average: explains relative, absolute and fixed but is vague about sticky or the containing block. Weak: mixes up relative and absolute or thinks absolute is always relative to the page.

question: A toolbar has `position: sticky; top: 0;` but it scrolls away with the page instead of sticking. Its ancestor `.layout` has `overflow: hidden;` to prevent horizontal scrolling. Why does sticky fail, and what else commonly stops it from working?
model_answer:
A sticky element sticks relative to its nearest scrolling ancestor, the closest ancestor that is a scroll container. overflow: hidden (like auto or scroll) makes .layout a scroll container, so the toolbar tries to stick inside .layout; but .layout itself never scrolls, the page does, so the threshold is never reached. Fix: remove the overflow from the ancestor, use `overflow: clip`, which clips without creating a scroll container, or deliberately make that ancestor the scrolling area with a fixed height.

Other common causes:
- No threshold is set; sticky needs top, bottom, left or right.
- The parent height is the same as the sticky element's. Sticky is confined to its parent, so there is no room to stick; move it into a taller parent.
- It is a flex or grid item stretched to the full height of its line: add `align-self: flex-start` (or `start` in grid).

expected_answer_points: Sticky works relative to the nearest scrolling ancestor | overflow hidden/auto/scroll on an ancestor creates a scroll container that never scrolls | Remove that overflow or use overflow: clip | A threshold such as top: 0 is required | The parent must be taller than the sticky element, because sticky is confined to it | Stretched flex or grid items need align-self: flex-start or start
common_mistakes: Blaming browser support for position: sticky | Switching to position: fixed and losing the element's place in the layout | Not checking the ancestors for overflow settings

question: A modal has `position: fixed; z-index: 9999;` yet it appears behind the site header, which has `position: sticky; z-index: 10;`. The modal is rendered inside `<main>`, and `main` has `position: relative; z-index: 1;`. Why does z-index 9999 lose, and how would you fix it?
model_answer:
z-index values are only compared within the same stacking context. Because main is positioned and has a z-index other than auto, it creates its own stacking context. Everything inside it, including the modal, is painted as part of main, and in the root stacking context main sits at level 1 while the header sits at level 10. So the whole of main, modal included, paints below the header; the 9999 only competes with main's other descendants.

Fixes:
- Render the modal outside main, as a direct child of body (a portal in React), so it joins the root stacking context.
- Remove z-index: 1 from main if it is not needed; position: relative without a z-index does not create a stacking context.
- Or use the native <dialog> element opened with showModal(), which renders in the browser's top layer above everything.
Also check ancestors for other stacking-context creators: transform, opacity below 1, filter, will-change, isolation: isolate and position: fixed or sticky.
keywords: stacking context, same stacking context, z-index: 1, root stacking context, portal, direct child of body, top layer, transform, opacity
expected_answer_points: z-index is only compared inside the same stacking context | main with position and z-index: 1 creates a stacking context | The modal is trapped at main's level (1), below the header's level (10) | Move the modal to be a direct child of body, e.g. with a portal | Or remove the ancestor's z-index, or use <dialog> in the top layer | transform, opacity below 1, filter and will-change also create stacking contexts

question: What is the difference between Flexbox and CSS Grid, and how do you decide which one to use for a layout?
model_answer: Flexbox is one-dimensional: it lays items out along a single axis, a row or a column, and sizing is mostly content-driven, so it suits components such as navbars, toolbars, button groups, centring and simple wrapping lists. Grid is two-dimensional: it defines rows and columns at the same time, so items line up in both directions and can be placed into named areas; it suits page layouts, dashboards, card galleries and forms with aligned labels. A useful rule: if you need alignment across rows and columns, use Grid; if items just need to flow and share space in one direction, use Flexbox. With flex-wrap, wrapped items do not line up with the row above, which is a sign Grid fits better. The two combine well: Grid for the page skeleton, Flexbox inside each card.
keywords: one-dimensional, two-dimensional, rows and columns, content-driven, components, page layouts, flex-wrap, combine

common_mistakes: Claiming Grid replaces Flexbox entirely | Saying Flexbox cannot lay items out in a column | Choosing by habit instead of by one- vs two-dimensional needs

question: Explain the difference between the CSS units px, %, em, rem, vw and vh. Which would you use for font sizes, and why?
model_answer: px is an absolute unit: a fixed CSS pixel that ignores the user's preferred font size. % is relative to the parent element: for width it is a share of the containing block's width, for font-size a share of the parent's font size. em is relative to the element's own font size (for font-size itself, the parent's), so nested em values compound. rem is relative to the root font size of the html element, 16px by default, so it never compounds. vw and vh are 1% of the viewport width and height; on phones 100vh can be taller than the visible area, so dvh or svh are safer. For font sizes use rem: it scales predictably and respects the user's browser font-size setting, which matters for accessibility. em works well for padding that should scale with a component's text.
keywords: absolute unit, parent element, compound, root font size, viewport, rem for font sizes, accessibility, dvh
expected_answer_points: px is absolute and ignores the user's font-size preference | % is relative to the parent or containing block | em is relative to the element's font size and compounds when nested | rem is relative to the root font size and does not compound | vw/vh are percentages of the viewport; dvh handles mobile browser bars | Use rem for font sizes for accessibility and consistency
common_mistakes: Saying em and rem are the same | Using px for every font size, which ignores user font preferences | Thinking % always refers to the viewport

question: How do you make images and text scale smoothly across screen sizes without writing a breakpoint for every device? Which CSS properties or functions would you use?
model_answer: For media, `img, video { max-width: 100%; height: auto; }` lets images shrink with their container without distortion and never stretch past their natural size; aspect-ratio with object-fit: cover keeps thumbnails a consistent shape. For containers, use fluid widths with a cap, e.g. `width: min(100% - 2rem, 1200px); margin-inline: auto;`, plus flex and grid with fr and minmax. For text, `font-size: clamp(1.5rem, 1rem + 2vw, 2.5rem)` grows with the viewport but never goes below the minimum or above the maximum; mixing rem into the middle value keeps browser zoom working, whereas pure vw text does not scale with zoom. Spacing in rem or em scales with the text. Container queries (@container) let a component adapt to its own container's width instead of the viewport.
keywords: max-width: 100%, height: auto, object-fit, aspect-ratio, min(), clamp(), rem, container queries

question: You inherit an admin dashboard with a fixed 280px sidebar and a wide data table. On a 375px phone the sidebar covers most of the screen and the table makes the whole page scroll sideways. How would you make it responsive with CSS?
model_answer: I would restructure it mobile-first. On small screens the layout is a single column and the sidebar becomes an off-canvas drawer: position: fixed with transform: translateX(-100%), sliding in with a transition when a toggle class is added, or it collapses into a top bar with a menu button. From about 1024px a media query switches the wrapper to display: grid with grid-template-columns: 280px minmax(0, 1fr). The minmax(0, 1fr) track (or min-width: 0 on the main area) lets the content column shrink instead of being pushed wider by the table. The table goes inside a wrapper with overflow-x: auto so only the table scrolls, not the page; for key screens I would hide low-priority columns on phones or restack each row into a card layout. Finally I would check touch targets of about 44px, fixed widths and images, and test in DevTools device mode and on a real phone.

question: What is the difference between a CSS transition and a CSS animation, and when would you use each?
model_answer: A transition animates a property between two states when its value changes, so it needs a trigger such as :hover, :focus or a class added by JavaScript. It is defined with transition-property, transition-duration, transition-timing-function and transition-delay, runs once from the old value to the new one, and reverses when the state changes back. An animation is defined with @keyframes, which can describe multiple steps (0%, 50%, 100%); it starts on its own as soon as it is applied and can loop with animation-iteration-count: infinite, alternate direction, pause with animation-play-state and keep its end state with animation-fill-mode. Use transitions for simple interactive hover effects and open/close states, and animations for multi-step, looping or automatic effects such as loaders and pulses.
keywords: two states, trigger, state change, @keyframes, multiple steps, iteration-count, loop, hover effects
expected_answer_points: A transition animates between two states when a value changes | Transitions need a trigger such as :hover or a class change | Animations use @keyframes with multiple steps | Animations start automatically and can loop, alternate and pause | Transitions for simple interactions; animations for loaders and looping effects

question: A mobile side menu slides in by animating `left` from -300px to 0, and product cards grow on hover by animating `width` and `height`. Users on low-end phones report stuttering. Why does this happen, and how would you rework the animations?
model_answer:
The browser renders in stages: style, layout, paint and composite. Animating left, width, height, top or margin changes geometry, so every frame triggers layout (reflow) and repaint on the main thread, often for surrounding elements too; on a slow phone this cannot finish within the roughly 16ms frame budget, so frames drop. transform and opacity can usually be handled by the compositor, often on the GPU, without layout or paint.

Rework: animate the menu with transform: translateX(-100%) to translateX(0) and transition: transform 250ms ease-out; make the card hover use transform: scale(1.03) instead of changing its size, and use opacity for fades. Apply will-change: transform only to elements that are about to animate, because too many layers waste memory. Verify with the DevTools Performance panel and paint flashing, keep durations around 150-300ms, and respect prefers-reduced-motion.
keywords: layout, reflow, repaint, main thread, compositor, transform, opacity, translateX, will-change, Performance panel
expected_answer_points: Animating left, width or height triggers layout and paint on every frame | Main-thread work exceeds the frame budget on low-end devices | transform and opacity can run on the compositor without layout | Use translateX for the menu and scale for the card hover | Use will-change sparingly and profile with the Performance panel | Respect prefers-reduced-motion
common_mistakes: Adding will-change to every element on the page | Believing a JavaScript animation library fixes layout-triggering properties automatically | Blaming the device without profiling
follow_up_question: How would you use the DevTools Performance panel to prove that your change removed the layout work?
evaluation_notes: Strong: explains the rendering pipeline and why geometry properties cause reflow, reworks both animations with transform/opacity, and mentions will-change caution and profiling. Average: knows to use transform instead of left but cannot explain why. Weak: suggests shorter durations or blames the phone without changing the properties.

question: What is the difference between var, let and const in JavaScript?
model_answer: var is function-scoped (or global when declared outside a function), can be re-declared, and is hoisted and initialised to undefined, so it can be read before its declaration line. let and const (ES6) are block-scoped: they exist only inside the nearest { } block, cannot be re-declared in the same scope, and stay in the temporal dead zone until their declaration runs, so accessing them earlier throws a ReferenceError. let can be reassigned; const must be initialised when declared and cannot be reassigned, although an object or array held in a const can still be mutated. Modern code uses const by default, let when the value must change, and avoids var.

question: What are the primitive data types in JavaScript, and how are they different from objects?
model_answer: JavaScript has seven primitive types: string, number, bigint, boolean, undefined, null and symbol. Primitives are immutable and are copied and compared by value. Everything else is an object (including arrays, functions and dates), which is stored and compared by reference, so two variables can point to the same object. The typeof operator identifies types, with two quirks: typeof null returns 'object' (a historical bug) and typeof a function returns 'function'. undefined means a variable has not been assigned a value, while null is an intentional 'no value' set by the programmer.

question: What is the difference between == and === in JavaScript?
model_answer: === is the strict equality operator: it returns true only if both operands have the same type and the same value, with no conversion. == is the loose equality operator: if the types differ it applies type coercion first, so 5 == '5' and 0 == false are true, while 5 === '5' is false. For objects, both operators compare references, not contents, so {} === {} is false. Because coercion rules are hard to remember, the best practice is to always use ===, with one common exception: value == null checks for both null and undefined.

question: What are first-class functions and higher-order functions in JavaScript?
model_answer: JavaScript functions are first-class: they are values that can be stored in variables, kept in arrays or objects, passed as arguments and returned from other functions. A higher-order function is a function that takes another function as an argument, returns a function, or both. Built-in examples are map, filter, reduce, setTimeout and addEventListener, which all accept a callback; a helper like debounce(fn, delay) that returns a new function is also higher-order. They make code reusable and declarative, for example nums.filter(n => n > 0) instead of a manual loop.

question: Explain global scope, function scope and block scope in JavaScript. What is the scope chain?
model_answer: Scope decides where a variable can be accessed. Variables declared outside any function or block are in global scope and visible everywhere. Variables declared inside a function (with var, let or const) are in function scope and visible only in that function. let and const declared inside a { } block such as an if or for are in block scope; var ignores blocks. JavaScript uses lexical scope: what a function can access is fixed by where it is written, not where it is called. When a variable is used, the engine looks in the current scope, then each outer scope up to the global scope; this lookup path is the scope chain, and a ReferenceError is thrown if the name is not found.

question: What is a closure in JavaScript? Give a practical use case.
model_answer: A closure is a function bundled with references to the variables of the scope where it was created (its lexical environment), so it keeps access to those variables even after the outer function has returned. Every JavaScript function forms a closure. Practical uses: data privacy, such as a counter whose value cannot be changed from outside; function factories like makeMultiplier(2); and keeping state in event handlers, debounce and memoize. Example: function counter() { let count = 0; return () => ++count; } gives each counter its own private count. Because closures hold references, a long-lived closure can keep large objects in memory and cause a memory leak.

question: How are arrow functions different from regular functions?
model_answer: Arrow functions have a shorter syntax and an implicit return for single expressions, but the key differences are in behaviour. They do not have their own this; they use the this of the surrounding scope (lexical this), and call, apply or bind cannot change it. They have no arguments object (use rest parameters instead), cannot be used as constructors with new, and have no prototype property. This makes them ideal for callbacks inside methods, such as in setTimeout or array methods, but a poor choice for object methods or event handlers that need this to be the object or the element.

question: How is the value of this determined when a function is called? Explain the role of call, apply and bind.
model_answer: For regular functions, this is set at call time by how the function is called. 1) Called with new: this is the newly created object. 2) Called with call, apply or bind: this is the object passed explicitly. 3) Called as a method (obj.method()): this is obj, the object before the dot. 4) Called as a plain function: this is undefined in strict mode (including modules and classes) or the global object in sloppy mode. Arrow functions ignore these rules and use the this of their enclosing scope. call(thisArg, a, b) invokes immediately with arguments listed individually, apply(thisArg, [a, b]) invokes immediately with an array of arguments, and bind(thisArg) returns a new function with this permanently fixed, useful for callbacks. A common bug is extracting a method (const f = obj.method; f()), which loses its this.

question: What is the difference between map() and forEach() on arrays? When would you use filter() or reduce() instead?
model_answer: forEach() runs a callback for each element and always returns undefined; it is used for side effects such as logging or updating the DOM. map() runs a callback for each element and returns a new array of the same length containing the callback's return values; it does not mutate the original array, so it is used to transform data and can be chained. filter() returns a new array with only the elements for which the callback returns a truthy value, and reduce() combines all elements into a single value, such as a sum or a lookup object, using an accumulator. None of them can be stopped early with break; use for...of, some() or find() when you need to stop.

question: A developer sorts prices with prices.sort() and gets [10, 100, 25, 5] from [25, 100, 5, 10]. Why, and how do you fix it?
model_answer:
Without a compare function, sort() converts the elements to strings and compares them in UTF-16 code-unit order, so '100' comes before '25' and '5' comes last. The fix is a numeric compare function that returns a negative, zero or positive number:

prices.sort((a, b) => a - b); // [5, 10, 25, 100]
prices.sort((a, b) => b - a); // descending

sort() also mutates the original array and returns the same array. If the original must stay unchanged, use prices.toSorted((a, b) => a - b) (ES2023) or [...prices].sort((a, b) => a - b).

question: Explain prototypal inheritance in JavaScript. How does the class syntax relate to prototypes?
model_answer: Every object has an internal link, [[Prototype]], to another object (read it with Object.getPrototypeOf). When you read a property that is not on the object itself, JavaScript looks it up along this prototype chain until it finds it or reaches null. Methods are therefore shared: every array gets map() from Array.prototype instead of having its own copy. Functions have a prototype property, and objects created with new Fn() get Fn.prototype as their prototype. ES6 class syntax is mostly syntactic sugar over this model: class methods are stored on Class.prototype, and extends links the child's prototype to the parent's, with super calling the parent constructor or methods. Object.create(proto) creates an object with a chosen prototype directly.

question: What is destructuring in JavaScript? Show array and object destructuring with a default value and a renamed variable.

question: What is the difference between the spread operator and rest parameters, since both use the ... syntax?
model_answer: They look the same but do opposite jobs. Spread expands an iterable or object into individual elements: Math.max(...nums), [...a, ...b] to merge arrays, or { ...user, age: 30 } to copy an object and override a property. Rest collects multiple values into one array or object: function sum(...nums) gathers all function arguments into a real array, and const { password, ...safeUser } = user collects the remaining properties. Rest must be the last parameter or element. A simple rule: spread is used where values are consumed (calls, array and object literals), rest is used where values are received (parameters and destructuring).

question: You are splitting a browser app into ES modules. How do you export and import code with named and default exports, and what must change in the HTML for it to work?
model_answer: Use named exports for several values per file (export function formatPrice() {} or export { a, b }) and at most one default export (export default class Cart {}). In the HTML, load the entry file with <script type="module" src="main.js"></script>. Modules are deferred by default, run in strict mode, have their own module scope (top-level variables are not global) and are evaluated only once however often they are imported. Without a bundler, relative paths need the file extension, and the page must be served over HTTP by a local dev server, because browsers such as Chrome block module scripts loaded from file:// (a CORS error). A dynamic import('./chart.js') loads a module lazily and returns a promise.

question: What is a callback function, and what is callback hell?
model_answer: A callback is a function passed as an argument to another function, to be called later, either synchronously (as in array.map(fn)) or asynchronously when an operation finishes (as in setTimeout(fn, 1000) or addEventListener('click', fn)). Callbacks were the original way to handle asynchronous results. Callback hell, also called the pyramid of doom, happens when several dependent async steps are nested inside each other's callbacks, giving deeply indented code that is hard to read and debug, with error handling repeated at every level. It is reduced with named functions and solved in modern code with Promises and async/await.

common_mistakes: Saying all callbacks are asynchronous | Defining callback hell as simply using many callbacks | Not mentioning Promises or async/await as the fix

question: What is a Promise in JavaScript, and what states can it be in?
model_answer: A Promise is an object that represents the eventual result of an asynchronous operation. It starts in the pending state and settles once, either fulfilled with a value or rejected with a reason (usually an Error); after that its state never changes. You consume it with .then() for the result, .catch() for errors and .finally() for cleanup that runs either way. Because then() returns a new promise, steps can be chained instead of nested, and one catch() at the end handles an error from any earlier step. new Promise((resolve, reject) => { ... }) creates one, although most APIs, such as fetch, already return promises.

question: What is the difference between Promise.all, Promise.allSettled, Promise.race and Promise.any?
model_answer: All four take an iterable of promises and return a new promise. Promise.all fulfils with an array of all results in input order, but rejects as soon as any one rejects (fail-fast); use it when every result is required. Promise.allSettled waits for every promise and fulfils with an array of { status, value } or { status, reason } objects; it never rejects, so it suits independent tasks where partial success is acceptable. Promise.race settles with the first promise to settle, whether it fulfils or rejects, and is often used to implement a timeout. Promise.any fulfils with the first fulfilled value and rejects with an AggregateError only if all of them reject.

question: How does async/await work, and how is it related to Promises?
model_answer: async/await (ES2017) is syntactic sugar over Promises. An async function always returns a promise: a returned value becomes the fulfilled value and a thrown error becomes the rejection. Inside it, await pauses only that function until the awaited promise settles, then resumes with the value or throws the rejection reason, so errors are handled with ordinary try/catch. await is non-blocking: while the function is paused, the rest of the program and the UI keep running, and the continuation is scheduled as a microtask. Consecutive awaits run one after another, so independent operations should be started together with Promise.all. await works inside async functions and as top-level await in ES modules.

question: Explain the JavaScript event loop. How do the call stack, the task (macrotask) queue and the microtask queue work together?
model_answer: JavaScript runs on a single thread with one call stack where synchronous code executes. Asynchronous work such as timers, network requests and DOM events is handled by the browser's Web APIs, which queue a callback when it is ready. Timer, I/O and event callbacks go to the task (macrotask) queue; promise reactions (then/catch/finally, code after await) and queueMicrotask callbacks go to the microtask queue. When the call stack is empty, the event loop runs one task, then runs all microtasks until the microtask queue is empty (including ones added meanwhile), and then the browser may render. So promise callbacks always run before setTimeout(fn, 0), and a long synchronous task or an endless microtask chain is blocking: it delays rendering and freezes the page.
keywords: single thread, call stack, Web APIs, macrotask queue, microtask queue, setTimeout, rendering, blocking

common_mistakes: Saying setTimeout(fn, 0) runs immediately | Saying JavaScript runs async code on multiple threads | Putting promise callbacks in the same queue as timers

model_answer: The order is 1, 4, 6, 3, 5, 2. question: A report page appends 10,000 table rows one at a time inside a loop, and in the same loop reads each row's offsetHeight to update a running total. The browser freezes for several seconds. What is causing it and how would you fix it?
model_answer: Two problems combine. Each appendChild into the live document is a separate DOM change, and reading offsetHeight right after a change forces the browser to recalculate layout synchronously (a forced reflow). Alternating writes and reads in a loop causes layout thrashing: thousands of layout passes on the main thread. Fixes: build all rows in a DocumentFragment (or off-document) and append once, so layout runs once; batch reads and writes separately, or calculate values from the data instead of measuring every row; schedule visual updates with requestAnimationFrame; and for very large tables use pagination or virtualisation, rendering only the visible rows. The DevTools Performance panel confirms the problem, as it flags forced reflows.

question: What is the difference between event.preventDefault() and event.stopPropagation()? Give an example of when you would use each.
model_answer: preventDefault() cancels the browser's default action for the event but lets the event continue through the DOM; for example, stopping a form submit from reloading the page so the data can be sent with fetch, or stopping a link from navigating. stopPropagation() stops the event from reaching further elements in its capturing or bubbling path but does not cancel the default action; for example, a click on a delete button inside a clickable card should not also trigger the card's click handler. stopImmediatePropagation() additionally blocks other listeners on the same element. Use stopPropagation sparingly, since it can break event delegation and analytics listeners higher up the tree.

question: What is event bubbling? Explain the three phases of event propagation.
model_answer: When an event happens on an element, it travels through the DOM in three phases. In the capturing phase it moves from window down through the ancestors towards the target. In the target phase it reaches the element where it happened. In the bubbling phase it travels back up from the target through each ancestor to document and window, running their listeners for the same event type. addEventListener listens in the bubbling phase by default; passing { capture: true } (or true) as the third argument listens during capturing. Inside a handler, event.target is the element where the event started, while event.currentTarget is the element whose listener is running. Most events bubble, but some, such as focus, blur, mouseenter and mouseleave, do not.

common_mistakes: Saying events bubble down from parent to child | Confusing target with currentTarget | Thinking every event bubbles

If the inner listener calls e.stopPropagation(), the event stops after the target phase, so only 'outer capture' and 'inner' are logged; the capture listener has already run because capturing happens before the target is reached.

question: What is event delegation, and why is it useful?
model_answer: Event delegation means attaching a single listener to a common parent element instead of one listener on every child, and relying on event bubbling to receive the children's events. Inside the handler, event.target, usually with target.closest('selector'), identifies which child was actually clicked, and the handler checks that the match is inside the parent before acting. Benefits: far fewer listeners and less memory for large lists, simpler code, and it automatically works for dynamic elements added later, because the parent's listener already exists. It is common for lists, tables, menus and todo apps. Limitations: it depends on bubbling, so events such as focus need focusin instead, and a stopPropagation call in a child breaks it.

question: On slow mobile networks, a product page sometimes shows its loading spinner forever because a fetch request never finishes, and fetch() has no timeout option. How would you add a timeout, tell a timeout apart from other errors, and retry safely?
model_answer: A request can hang for a very long time, so the page must set its own limit with an abort signal: fetch(url, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(8000) }) rejects with a TimeoutError DOMException after 8 seconds. In older code, create an AbortController, call controller.abort() from a setTimeout and clear that timer when the response arrives; that version rejects with an AbortError. In the catch block, check err.name: 'TimeoutError' means show a 'network is slow, try again' message, 'AbortError' means the request was cancelled on purpose and can be ignored, and a TypeError means a network failure. Hide the spinner in finally so it stops on every path. Retry only safe requests such as GET, a limited number of times (for example 3) with exponential backoff (1 s, 2 s, 4 s), and do not retry 4xx responses; blindly retrying a POST could create duplicate records.

question: What is the difference between localStorage and sessionStorage? What are their main limitations?
model_answer: Both are Web Storage APIs that store string key-value pairs per origin, with the same methods: setItem, getItem, removeItem, clear and key. localStorage persists until it is cleared by code or by the user, and is shared by all tabs and windows of the same origin. sessionStorage lasts only for the lifetime of the tab: it survives reloads but is cleared when the tab is closed, and each tab has its own copy. Limitations: values are strings only, so objects need JSON.stringify and JSON.parse; capacity is small, typically about 5 MB per origin; the API is synchronous and can block the main thread with large data; and, unlike cookies, the data is never sent to the server automatically.

question: How does try...catch...finally work in JavaScript, and how do you throw your own errors?
model_answer: Code that might fail goes in the try block. If an exception is thrown, execution jumps to catch, which receives the error object (with name, message and stack); if nothing is thrown, catch is skipped. finally runs in both cases, even after a return, so it is used for cleanup such as hiding a loading spinner. You raise your own errors with throw new Error('Invalid email'). It is best to throw Error objects, or subclasses such as TypeError or a custom error class like class ValidationError extends Error, rather than strings, so a stack trace is available and errors can be told apart with instanceof. try...catch only catches synchronous errors, or rejections of promises that are awaited inside the try block.

question: How do you debug JavaScript in the browser? Which DevTools features do you use?
model_answer: Start with the Console: read the error message and stack trace, and click the file:line link to jump to the source. Use console.log, console.table for arrays of objects, console.error and console.dir to inspect values. In the Sources panel, set breakpoints (or add a debugger statement) to pause execution, then step over, step into and step out while watching variables, the call stack and scope; conditional breakpoints and event-listener breakpoints help with rare cases. Use the Network tab to check request URLs, status codes, headers and response bodies, the Elements panel to inspect the DOM, and the Application panel to view localStorage. Source maps let you debug the original code of bundled builds.

question: A single-page dashboard becomes slower and uses more memory the longer it stays open. Every time the user switches between sections, widgets are removed and recreated. Which JavaScript causes would you suspect, and how would you find and fix them?
model_answer: This looks like a memory leak: references keep old widgets alive after they are removed. Likely causes are event listeners added to window or document on every render but never removed; setInterval timers or polling that keep running after a widget is gone; closures or global caches (arrays, Maps) that keep growing and hold detached DOM nodes; and requests that finish later and update widgets that no longer exist. To find them, use the DevTools Memory panel: take heap snapshots before and after switching sections several times and compare them, looking for growing object counts and detached elements; the Performance monitor shows listener and DOM node counts. Fix it by giving each widget a cleanup function that calls removeEventListener, clearInterval and abort() on an AbortController, and by using event delegation, a WeakMap for per-element data and bounded caches.

common_mistakes: Blaming the garbage collector itself | Only suggesting a page reload as the fix | Not knowing how to confirm a leak with heap snapshots

question: What is React, and what are its main features?
model_answer: React is an open-source JavaScript library, maintained by Meta, for building user interfaces out of reusable components. Its main features are a component-based architecture; declarative UI, where you describe what the screen should look like for the current state and React updates the DOM for you; JSX syntax; one-way data flow from parent to child through props; a virtual DOM with efficient reconciliation; and hooks that give function components state and side effects. React is a UI library rather than a full framework, so routing and data fetching usually come from other libraries such as React Router.

question: What is the virtual DOM, and how does React use it to update the page?
model_answer: The virtual DOM is an in-memory representation of the UI: a tree of plain JavaScript objects (React elements) that describes what should be on screen. When state or props change, React re-renders the affected components to build a new tree, compares it with the previous tree (this diffing process is called reconciliation), and then commits only the minimal set of changes to the real DOM. Because real DOM updates, layout and repaint are relatively expensive, applying only what changed keeps updates fast, and developers never write manual DOM-manipulation code.
keywords: in-memory representation, React elements, re-render, diffing, reconciliation, minimal changes, real DOM
expected_answer_points: The virtual DOM is an in-memory JavaScript representation of the UI | A state or props change produces a new virtual tree | React diffs the new tree against the previous one (reconciliation) | Only the minimal changes are applied to the real DOM | Fewer real DOM operations make updates efficient

question: What is a component in React, and what rules must a function component follow?
model_answer: A component is an independent, reusable piece of UI. In modern React it is a JavaScript function that receives a props object and returns JSX describing what to render (or null to render nothing). Rules: its name must start with a capital letter, otherwise JSX treats it as an HTML tag; it must be pure while rendering, meaning the same props and state give the same output and it does not mutate props or perform side effects such as API calls in the render body; and hooks may only be called at its top level. Small components are combined through composition to build the whole application tree.

expected_answer_points: A component is a reusable, independent piece of UI | A function component takes props and returns JSX | Its name must start with a capital letter | It must be pure during rendering: no mutating props, no side effects | Components are composed together to build the UI tree
common_mistakes: Naming a component in lowercase so React treats it as an HTML tag | Modifying props inside the component | Making API calls directly in the component body

question: What is JSX, and what happens to it before the code runs in the browser?
model_answer:
JSX is a syntax extension for JavaScript that lets you write HTML-like markup inside JavaScript to describe UI. Browsers cannot run it, so a compiler such as Babel, SWC or esbuild (run by the build tool, for example Vite) transpiles every JSX element into a function call. With the modern JSX transform,

Hi

becomes jsx('h1', { className: 'title', children: 'Hi' }); older setups produced React.createElement calls. Each call returns a React element, a plain object describing the UI. JSX differs from HTML: attributes are camelCase (className, onClick), JavaScript expressions go inside curly braces {}, and every tag must be closed.

question: What is the difference between props and state in React?
model_answer: Props are inputs passed from a parent component to a child, much like function arguments. They are read-only inside the child and change only when the parent re-renders with new values. State is data managed internally by the component itself, created with useState or useReducer, that changes over time, usually in response to user actions or API responses. Calling the state setter function triggers a re-render of that component and its children. The two work together: a parent's state is often passed down to children as props, which gives React its one-way data flow.

question:
In this list the delete function runs for every item as soon as the page renders, and clicking the button does nothing useful. Why, and how do you fix it?

<button onClick={handleDelete(item.id)}>Delete</button>

React event props expect a function reference that React calls later, when the event fires. Fix it by passing a function, typically an arrow function that captures the argument:

When no argument is needed, pass the reference directly: onClick={handleSave}. If the called function sets state, calling it during render can even cause a 'Too many re-renders' error. question: What are the common ways to render content conditionally in React?
model_answer: Because JSX is JavaScript, you use normal JavaScript conditions. An if statement with an early return suits larger branches, for example if (loading) return <Spinner />. The logical AND operator, cond && <A />, renders something or nothing, but the left side should be a boolean condition: {items.length && <List />} renders 0 on screen when the array is empty, so write items.length > 0 && <List />. Returning null renders nothing. For many states, a switch or a lookup object in a helper keeps JSX readable.

question: Why does React need keys when rendering lists, and why is using the array index as the key risky?
model_answer: Keys give each list item a stable identity. During reconciliation React uses them to match the items of the new render with those of the previous render and decide which elements to keep, move, insert or remove. If the array index is the key and items are inserted, deleted, sorted or filtered, the indexes shift, so React reuses the wrong component instance: component state such as a typed input value or a checked box ends up on the wrong item, and more DOM updates happen than needed. Use a stable unique id from the data; the index is acceptable only for a static list that never reorders or changes. Keys only need to be unique among siblings.

expected_answer_points: Keys give list items a stable identity | React uses keys during reconciliation to match old and new items | Index keys change when items are inserted, deleted or reordered | State such as input values then attaches to the wrong item | Use a stable unique id; the index only for static lists

question: What is a controlled component in React?
model_answer: A controlled component is a form element, such as an input, textarea or select, whose value is driven by React state instead of by the DOM. You pass the state as the value prop (or checked for checkboxes) and update that state in an onChange handler, so React state is the single source of truth. Example: <input value={email} onChange={e => setEmail(e.target.value)} />. Because every change goes through state, it is easy to add validation while typing, format input, enable or disable the submit button, and reset the form by setting state.

question: How do controlled and uncontrolled components differ, and when would you choose an uncontrolled input?
model_answer: In a controlled component React state holds the value (value plus onChange), so every keystroke updates state and re-renders, giving instant validation and full control. In an uncontrolled component the DOM keeps the value: you set the starting value with defaultValue and read the current value only when needed, through a ref created with useRef or from FormData when the form is submitted. Uncontrolled inputs need less code and cause fewer re-renders, which suits simple forms and integration with non-React widgets. A file input is always uncontrolled because its value can only be set by the user. Choose controlled inputs when the UI must react to each change, such as live validation, dependent fields or formatting.

question: What are hooks in React, and what are the rules of hooks?
model_answer: Hooks are functions with a use prefix that let function components use React features such as state (useState), side effects (useEffect), context (useContext) and refs (useRef) without writing classes. There are two rules. First, call hooks only at the top level of a component or custom hook, never inside conditions, loops or nested functions. Second, call them only from React function components or custom hooks, not from regular JavaScript functions. React identifies each hook's state by its call order, so the order must be identical on every render. The eslint-plugin-react-hooks linter enforces these rules.

question: What is useEffect used for, and how does its dependency array control when it runs?
model_answer: useEffect runs side effects after React has rendered and committed the changes to the screen, for example fetching data, subscribing to events, starting timers or synchronizing with a non-React widget. The dependency array controls re-running: with no array the effect runs after every render; with an empty array [] it runs only once after the first render (on mount); with values such as [userId] it runs after the first render and again whenever any listed value changes, compared with Object.is. The effect can return a cleanup function, which React calls before the effect runs again and when the component unmounts.

question: What is the cleanup function in useEffect, when does it run, and why does React 18 Strict Mode run effects twice in development?
model_answer: The cleanup function is the function you return from an effect. React calls it before running the effect again when dependencies change, and when the component unmounts. It undoes whatever the effect set up: calling removeEventListener, clearing timers with clearInterval, closing a WebSocket, unsubscribing, or aborting a fetch with AbortController. Without cleanup you get memory leaks, duplicate listeners and state updates from outdated requests. In development, React 18 Strict Mode mounts each component, unmounts it and mounts it again, so every effect runs setup, cleanup and setup again. This development-only behavior deliberately exposes effects with missing cleanup; it does not happen in production builds.

question: How do the class lifecycle methods componentDidMount, componentDidUpdate and componentWillUnmount map to hooks in function components?
model_answer: Function components have no lifecycle methods; the same behavior is expressed with useEffect. componentDidMount corresponds to useEffect(() => {...}, []) with an empty dependency array, which runs once after mount. componentDidUpdate corresponds to an effect with dependencies, useEffect(() => {...}, [userId]), which runs when those dependencies change (unlike componentDidUpdate, it also runs after mount). componentWillUnmount corresponds to the cleanup function returned from an effect. Other mappings: this.state and setState become useState, and shouldComponentUpdate becomes React.memo. The better mental model is synchronization rather than lifecycle events: each effect keeps something outside React in sync with the current props and state.

question: What is the difference between useRef and useState, and what are the two main uses of useRef?
model_answer: Both persist a value across renders, but updating state with its setter schedules a re-render, while changing ref.current does not: a ref is a mutable box that React does not watch. Use state for data the UI displays. useRef has two main uses. First, accessing a DOM node, for example <input ref={inputRef} /> and then inputRef.current.focus() inside an effect or event handler. Second, storing mutable values that must not trigger a render, such as a timer id, an AbortController or a flag. Avoid reading or writing ref.current during rendering, because the screen would not update when it changes.

question: How do you set up client-side routing with React Router v6 for a Home page, an About page and a 'page not found' page?
model_answer:
Install react-router-dom, wrap the app in BrowserRouter, and declare each Route inside Routes with a path and an element prop:

import { BrowserRouter, Routes, Route, Link } from 'react-router-dom';

<BrowserRouter>
  <nav><Link to="/">Home</Link> <Link to="/about">About</Link></nav>
  <Routes>
    <Route path="/" element={<Home />} />
    <Route path="/about" element={<About />} />
    <Route path="*" element={<NotFound />} />
  </Routes>
</BrowserRouter>

BrowserRouter uses the History API, so the URL changes without a page reload. Routes picks the best match, and path="*" is a catch-all route for unknown URLs. createBrowserRouter with RouterProvider is the data-router alternative that also supports loaders and actions.

question: What is the difference between <Link>, a plain <a href> and useNavigate for navigation in React Router?
model_answer: A plain <a href> makes the browser request a new document, which causes a full page reload, restarts the React app and loses all its state. <Link to="/cart"> renders an anchor but intercepts the click and updates the URL through the History API, so React Router renders the new route with client-side navigation and no reload; NavLink also adds an active class. useNavigate returns a function for programmatic navigation from code, for example after a successful login: navigate('/dashboard'), navigate('/login', { replace: true }) to replace the current history entry, or navigate(-1) to go back. question: Design the client-side authentication for a React app that talks to a REST API using a JWT. How would you store the auth state, make it available to components, attach the token to requests, and handle page refresh and logout?
model_answer:
1. Create an AuthContext with an AuthProvider near the root that holds user, token (or only user when the backend uses an httpOnly cookie), a loading flag, and login and logout functions. Components read it through a useAuth() custom hook instead of props.
2. login calls the API, saves the user and token in state, and navigates back to the page the user came from.
3. All requests go through one API module (a fetch wrapper or an Axios instance with an interceptor) that adds the Authorization header as 'Bearer <token>' and calls logout on a 401 response.
4. A page refresh wipes React state, so the provider must restore the session on mount, for example by calling /api/me with the cookie or a persisted token, and keeps loading true until that check finishes so routes do not redirect too early.
5. logout clears state, stored tokens and cached user data, then redirects to /login.
6. Private pages sit under a ProtectedRoute layout route (optionally checking roles), while the server still performs server-side checks of the token and role on every request, because client-side checks only improve the user experience.

question: After User A logs out and User B logs in on the same browser, User B briefly sees User A's name and cart items, and pressing the browser Back button right after logout shows A's dashboard again. What is wrong in the React app, and how would you fix it?
model_answer: Logout only removed the token, but user data still lives in memory: the AuthContext user, cart state in Context or Redux, and cached API responses (for example in React Query). React never reloaded, so those values survive until something overwrites them. Fix it with one logout function that clears everything: set the auth user to null, remove the stored token, reset global stores (dispatch a reset action or call queryClient.clear()), and then navigate('/login', { replace: true }) so the dashboard is replaced in history. Protected routes must read the auth state on every render, so if Back does reach a dashboard route it redirects to login instead of showing old screens. Giving the app shell key={user?.id} remounts it for a new user so no component keeps old local state. The backend must also stop accepting the old token.

expected_answer_points: Logout cleared only the token; user data remains in memory (context, stores, cache) | One logout function must reset auth state, token storage, global stores and cached API data | Navigate to login with replace so the protected page is not kept in history | Protected routes re-check the auth state and redirect when logged out | Remounting with a key tied to the user removes leftover component state | The backend must also stop accepting the old token

question: A product page has a SearchBar component and a sibling ProductList component. Typing in the search bar should filter the list. Where should the search text live, and how do the two components communicate?
model_answer: Sibling components cannot read each other's state, so I would lift the state up to their closest common parent. The parent owns const [query, setQuery] = useState(''), passes query and an onQueryChange callback to SearchBar as props, and passes query (or the already filtered list) to ProductList. When the user types, SearchBar calls the callback prop, the parent's state updates, and both children re-render with the new value. This keeps a single source of truth and one-way data flow. Only if many distant components needed the value would I move it into Context or a state library.

question: Why can putting frequently changing data into one large React Context hurt performance, and how would you reduce the problem?
model_answer: When a Provider's value changes (compared with Object.is), every consumer that calls useContext for that context will re-render, even if it uses only a part of the value that did not change, and wrapping a consumer in React.memo does not stop it. If the value is written inline, as in value={{ user, cart }}, a new object is created on every Provider render, so consumers re-render even when nothing changed. To reduce this: memoize the value with useMemo and its functions with useCallback; split one big context into smaller ones by concern and update frequency (AuthContext, ThemeContext, CartContext), or put state and dispatch in separate contexts; keep fast-changing local state such as form input out of context; and for large, frequently updated global state use a store such as Redux Toolkit, whose selectors re-render only the components whose selected data changed.
keywords: consumers re-render, Object.is, new object, useMemo, split contexts, state and dispatch, selectors, Redux Toolkit
expected_answer_points: Every consumer re-renders when the Provider value changes | An inline object value is a new reference on each Provider render | Memoize the value with useMemo and callbacks with useCallback | Split contexts by concern or update frequency, for example state vs dispatch | Keep fast-changing local state out of context | Use a store with selectors, such as Redux Toolkit, for large frequently updated state
common_mistakes: Believing React.memo prevents re-renders caused by context | Putting all application state into a single context | Treating Context as a full state management library rather than a way to pass values down
follow_up_question: How does useSelector in Redux Toolkit avoid re-rendering components whose data did not change?
evaluation_notes: Strong: explains consumer re-renders on value change, the inline-object trap, and several mitigations (memoized value, split contexts, selectors). Average: knows consumers re-render and suggests useMemo only. Weak: claims Context has no performance cost or suggests React.memo as the fix.

question: When would you choose Redux Toolkit over React Context with useReducer for global state?
model_answer: Context with useReducer is built in and works well for small or rarely changing global state, such as the logged-in user, theme or language. I would choose Redux Toolkit when the app has large, frequently updated state shared by many components, complex update logic, or a big team that benefits from a strict structure. It offers a single store split into slices; createSlice generates action creators and uses Immer, so reducers can be written in a 'mutating' style safely; useSelector subscribes components to just the data they select, so only affected components re-render; and it includes middleware, the Redux DevTools with time-travel debugging, and RTK Query for fetching and caching server data. The trade-off is an extra dependency and more setup. Redux Toolkit is the recommended way to write Redux today, not hand-written reducers with legacy createStore.

question: You are structuring the state of an e-commerce React app with a product listing, filters, a cart, the logged-in user and a checkout form. Where would each kind of state live, and why?
model_answer:
I would classify state by who needs it and where it comes from.
1. Server state (products, product details, orders) comes from the API and needs caching, loading and refetching. Fetch it with custom hooks, ideally using TanStack Query or RTK Query, instead of copying it into a global store by hand.
2. URL state (search text, category, sort, page) goes in the query string with useSearchParams, so filters survive a refresh and can be shared as a link.
3. Global client state: the logged-in user lives in an AuthContext; the cart, used by the header badge, cart page and checkout, lives in a CartContext with useReducer, or in Redux Toolkit if it grows or updates often, and is persisted to localStorage or the server.
4. Local state (checkout form fields, an open modal, the selected tab) stays in the component with useState, lifted only to the closest common parent when shared.
5. Derived state such as the cart total or the filtered list is computed during render (with useMemo if expensive), never stored separately.
Keeping each piece of state at the lowest level that needs it avoids unnecessary re-renders and duplicated, out-of-sync data.

question: What is the difference between React.memo, useMemo and useCallback, and when should you use each?
model_answer: React.memo is a higher-order component: it wraps a component and skips re-rendering it when the new props pass a shallow comparison with the previous props. useMemo is a hook that caches a computed value between renders and recalculates it only when its dependencies change, for example const sorted = useMemo(() => sortProducts(list), [list]). useCallback caches a function itself; useCallback(fn, deps) is equivalent to useMemo(() => fn, deps), so the same function reference is passed to children. They are often combined: useCallback and useMemo keep props referentially stable so that a React.memo child can actually skip rendering. Use them for an expensive calculation or props of memoized children, ideally after profiling shows a problem; applied everywhere they add complexity without benefit.
keywords: higher-order component, shallow comparison, computed value, dependencies, function reference, referentially stable, expensive calculation, profiling
expected_answer_points: React.memo wraps a component and skips re-rendering when props are shallowly equal | useMemo caches a computed value until its dependencies change | useCallback caches a function reference until its dependencies change | useCallback and useMemo keep props stable so memoized children can skip rendering | Use them for expensive work or after profiling, not everywhere
common_mistakes: Thinking useMemo memoizes a whole component | Wrapping every function in useCallback by default | Believing React.memo deep-compares props

question: How would you use React.lazy and Suspense to reduce the initial bundle size of an app with heavy Admin and Reports pages?
model_answer:
By default the bundler puts every imported page into the main bundle. React.lazy with a dynamic import() makes the bundler put a component into a separate chunk that is downloaded only when it is first rendered, and Suspense shows a fallback while the chunk loads. Route-level splitting is the usual starting point:

import { lazy, Suspense } from 'react';

const Admin = lazy(() => import('./pages/Admin'));
const Reports = lazy(() => import('./pages/Reports'));

<Suspense fallback={<Spinner />}>
  <Routes>
    <Route path="/admin" element={<Admin />} />
    <Route path="/reports" element={<Reports />} />
  </Routes>
</Suspense>

This code splitting gives a faster initial load. The lazy module needs a default export, lazy must be called at module level (not inside a component), and an error boundary should catch a failed chunk download.
keywords: code splitting, dynamic import, separate chunk, fallback, route-level splitting, initial load, default export, error boundary
expected_answer_points: React.lazy with dynamic import() creates a separate chunk | The chunk is downloaded only when the component first renders | Suspense shows a fallback while it loads | Split at route level for heavy pages | The lazy module needs a default export and lazy is declared at module level | An error boundary handles failed chunk loads
common_mistakes: Calling lazy inside the component body, which recreates the component and loses its state | Forgetting the Suspense boundary | Lazy-loading tiny components, adding requests without benefit
follow_up_question: How would you start loading the Reports chunk early, when the user hovers over its link?

question: A transactions page renders 10,000 rows, and typing in its filter box freezes the page for about a second on every keystroke. How would you investigate and fix it?
model_answer: First measure with the React DevTools Profiler to see which components render and how long they take. The usual causes are 10,000 DOM rows and re-filtering the whole list on every keystroke. question: Which tools and techniques would you use to debug a React component that is showing the wrong data?

question: What is the difference between the JDK, the JRE and the JVM?
model_answer: The JVM (Java Virtual Machine) is the runtime engine that loads .class files, verifies the bytecode and executes it with an interpreter and a JIT compiler; it also manages memory and garbage collection. The JRE (Java Runtime Environment) is the JVM plus the core class libraries needed to run a program. The JDK (Java Development Kit) is the JRE plus development tools such as javac, jar, javadoc and jshell, so developers need the JDK to compile code. Since Java 11 there is no separate JRE installer from Oracle; you install a JDK, and jlink can build a trimmed runtime. Because javac produces platform-neutral bytecode that any JVM can run, Java programs are platform independent, while each JVM itself is platform specific.
keywords: JVM, JRE, JDK, bytecode, class libraries, javac, JIT compiler, platform independent
expected_answer_points: JVM loads and executes bytecode and manages memory/garbage collection | JRE = JVM + core class libraries needed to run programs | JDK = JRE + development tools such as javac, jar and jshell | Bytecode running on any JVM makes Java platform independent | The JIT compiler turns frequently used bytecode into native code
common_mistakes: Saying the JVM compiles .java source files (javac does that) | Claiming the JVM itself is platform independent | Treating the three as the same thing or reversing their nesting

model_answer: It prints true, false, true. Integer is a wrapper class, and assigning an int literal to it uses autoboxing, which calls Integer.valueOf(). By default valueOf() returns cached objects for values from -128 to 127, so a and b refer to the same object and == is true. 128 is outside the Integer cache, so c and d are two different objects; for objects == is a reference comparison, so it is false. equals() compares the wrapped int values, so it is true. The rule is to compare wrapper objects with equals() or after unboxing to int, never with ==.

question: Explain how Java uses stack and heap memory, and how garbage collection decides which objects to remove.
model_answer: Each thread has its own stack of method frames holding local variables, primitive values and references to objects; a frame is removed automatically when its method returns. All objects and arrays are allocated on the shared heap. The garbage collector frees heap objects that are no longer reachable from GC roots such as live thread stacks and static fields. Reachability, not reference counting, decides this, so objects that only reference each other in a cycle are still collected. Most collectors, including the default G1, split the heap into young and old generations because most objects die young. A StackOverflowError usually means very deep or infinite recursion, while an OutOfMemoryError means the heap is full of objects that are still reachable.
keywords: stack, heap, local variables, references, garbage collector, reachable, GC roots, StackOverflowError, OutOfMemoryError
expected_answer_points: Each thread has its own stack with method frames, local variables and references | Objects and arrays are allocated on the shared heap | The garbage collector removes objects that are not reachable from GC roots | Unreachable cycles are still collected (no reference counting) | Heap is usually generational: young and old generations | StackOverflowError relates to the stack; OutOfMemoryError to the heap
common_mistakes: Saying objects created inside a method are stored on the stack | Believing System.gc() forces an immediate collection | Thinking that setting a variable to null frees memory immediately

Average: correct stack/heap split but only says 'GC removes unused objects'. Weak: stores objects on the stack or cannot describe when an object is collected.

model_answer: It prints 50 10. Java is always pass-by-value. For the primitive n the method receives a copy of the value, so assigning 99 does not affect num. For the object, what is passed is a copy of the reference: b initially points to the same object as box, so b.value = 50 is a mutation of that shared Box and the caller sees it. The statement b = new Box() only reassigns the local copy of the reference, so setting 99 on the new object has no effect on box. That is why a method can modify an object passed to it but cannot make the caller's variable point to a different object.

question: What are the four pillars of object-oriented programming? Explain each briefly with a Java example.
model_answer: Encapsulation bundles data with the methods that use it and hides state behind private fields, e.g. a BankAccount whose balance changes only through deposit() and withdraw(). Inheritance lets a class reuse and extend another class with extends, e.g. SavingsAccount extends Account. Polymorphism means one reference type can take many forms: method overloading is resolved at compile time and method overriding at runtime, e.g. a Shape reference calling the correct area() for a Circle or a Rectangle. Abstraction exposes what an object does and hides how it does it, using abstract classes and interfaces, e.g. a PaymentMethod interface with a pay() method.

question: How are a class and an object related in Java? Walk through what happens when `Car car = new Car("Red");` runs.
model_answer: A class is a blueprint that declares fields (state) and methods (behaviour); an object is a concrete instance of that class created at runtime with its own copy of the instance fields, and many objects can be created from one class. When the statement runs, the Car class is loaded and initialised if this is its first use. The new keyword allocates memory for the object on the heap and sets every field to its default value (0, false or null). Field initialisers and the matching constructor Car(String) then run and set the colour to Red. Finally, a reference to the new object is stored in the local variable car, which lives on the stack; the variable holds the reference, not the object itself.

expected_answer_points: A class is a blueprint defining fields and methods | An object is a runtime instance with its own state | new allocates memory on the heap and sets default values | The constructor initialises the object | The variable stores a reference to the object

question: What is encapsulation, and how would you apply it to a BankAccount class?
model_answer: Encapsulation means bundling data and the methods that operate on it in one class and hiding the internal state, so other code can change it only through controlled access. In a BankAccount the balance field is private and there is no public setBalance(). Instead, public methods deposit() and withdraw() perform validation (positive amount, sufficient funds) before changing the balance, and a getter getBalance() gives read-only access. This data hiding protects invariants such as 'balance never goes negative' and lets the class change its internal representation later without breaking callers. Setters are added only where a change is genuinely allowed.

question: Why does Java not allow a class to extend more than one class, and how does it deal with the same problem for interfaces?
model_answer: Java supports single inheritance of classes to avoid the diamond problem: if class D could extend both B and C, and both overrode a method from A or carried their own state, there would be ambiguity about which implementation and which copy of the state D inherits. A class can implement multiple interfaces because interfaces carry no instance state. Since Java 8 interfaces can have default methods, so a conflict is still possible, and Java resolves it with rules: a method declared in the class or a superclass wins, then the more specific sub-interface wins, and if two unrelated interfaces provide the same default method the code does not compile until the class overrides it. The override can call a chosen version with InterfaceName.super.method().
keywords: single inheritance, diamond problem, ambiguity, multiple interfaces, default methods, override, InterfaceName.super
expected_answer_points: Classes support single inheritance only | Multiple class inheritance causes the diamond problem (ambiguity over methods and state) | A class can implement multiple interfaces | Default-method conflict rules: class wins, then the more specific interface | Unrelated conflicting defaults must be overridden; InterfaceName.super.method() picks one
common_mistakes: Saying Java has no multiple inheritance at all (it has multiple inheritance of type) | Not knowing that conflicting default methods cause a compile error | Saying interfaces cannot contain any method bodies in modern Java
