question: What is the difference between method overloading and method overriding?
model_answer: Overloading means methods in the same class share the same name but have different parameter lists (number, type or order of parameters). The compiler chooses the method from the argument types, so it is compile-time (static) polymorphism; a different return type alone does not create a valid overload. Overriding means a subclass provides its own implementation of an inherited instance method with the same signature. The JVM picks the implementation from the actual object at runtime through dynamic dispatch, so it is runtime polymorphism. An override may use a covariant return type, cannot reduce visibility or throw broader checked exceptions, and should be marked @Override. Static, private and final methods cannot be overridden.
keywords: same name, different parameter lists, compile-time polymorphism, same signature, runtime polymorphism, dynamic dispatch, @Override, covariant return type
expected_answer_points: Overloading: same name, different parameter lists, usually in the same class | Overloading is resolved at compile time (static polymorphism) | Overriding: subclass redefines an inherited method with the same signature | Overriding is resolved at runtime through dynamic dispatch | Override rules: covariant return, no weaker access, no broader checked exceptions, @Override | Static, private and final methods cannot be overridden
common_mistakes: Saying a different return type alone is a valid overload | Saying static methods can be overridden | Mixing up which one is resolved at compile time and which at runtime

question: What is the difference between an abstract class and an interface in modern Java (Java 17), and when would you choose each?
model_answer: An abstract class can have instance fields, constructors, concrete and abstract methods with any access modifier, and a class can extend only one of them (single inheritance). An interface defines a contract: its fields are implicitly public static final constants, it has no constructors or instance state, and a class can implement multiple interfaces. Since Java 8 interfaces can also contain default and static methods, and since Java 9 private methods, so the real difference today is state and inheritance. Choose an abstract class when closely related classes share state or common code, for example an abstract Account holding a balance. Choose an interface to describe a capability that unrelated classes can offer, such as Comparable or a PaymentMethod contract.

question: What is a constructor in Java, how is it different from a normal method, and what is constructor chaining?
model_answer: A constructor is a special block of code that runs when an object is created with the new keyword and is used to initialise its state. It has the same name as the class and no return type (not even void), it is not inherited, and it cannot be abstract, static or final. If a class declares no constructor, the compiler adds a no-argument default constructor; once you declare any constructor, that default is no longer generated. Constructor chaining means one constructor calling another: this(...) calls another constructor of the same class to reuse initialisation code, and super(...) calls a parent class constructor. In Java 17 either call must be the first statement, and if you write neither, the compiler inserts super() automatically.

common_mistakes: Giving a constructor a void return type, which turns it into a normal method | Expecting the default constructor to still exist after declaring a parameterised one | Saying constructors are inherited

question: Why is the main method declared as `public static void main(String[] args)`? Can it be overloaded?
model_answer: public lets the JVM call it from outside the class. static lets the JVM call it without creating an object of the class first. void means it returns nothing to the JVM; an exit code is set with System.exit() instead. String[] args receives the command-line arguments (String... args is also accepted). Yes, main can be overloaded like any other method, for example main(int x), but the JVM uses only the public static void main(String[]) signature as the entry point, so the other overloads run only if you call them yourself. Java 25 also allows simpler instance main methods, but the classic form is the standard in Java 17.

question: Explain the four access levels in Java (private, default, protected, public) and where each one is visible.
model_answer: private members are visible only inside the same class (including its nested classes). Default access, used when no modifier is written and also called package-private, makes a member visible to every class in the same package. protected members are visible in the same package and also to subclasses in other packages, through inheritance. public members are visible everywhere. From most to least restrictive the order is private, default, protected, public. A top-level class can only be public or package-private. Good encapsulation starts with private fields and widens access only when needed, and an overriding method may keep or widen the visibility of the method it overrides but never reduce it.

common_mistakes: Saying protected means subclasses only (it also includes the same package) | Thinking default access means public | Saying a top-level class can be private

question: What does the static keyword mean when it is applied to a variable, a method, a block and a nested class?
model_answer: static means the member belongs to the class rather than to any object. A static variable has one shared copy for all instances, for example a counter of how many objects were created. A static method is called through the class name, cannot use this, and can directly access only static members; utility methods such as Math.max are static. A static block runs once when the class is loaded and initialises static data. A static nested class does not need an instance of the outer class and cannot access the outer class's instance members directly. Static mutable state should be used carefully because it is shared by all threads and makes code harder to test.

question: What is the difference between final, finally and finalize() in Java?
model_answer: final is a modifier. A final variable can be assigned only once (a final reference cannot be reassigned, but the object it points to can still be modified), a final method cannot be overridden, and a final class such as String cannot be extended. finally is a block after try/catch that always executes, whether or not an exception is thrown, and is used for cleanup; it is skipped only in cases such as System.exit() or a JVM crash. finalize() is a method of Object that the garbage collector might call before reclaiming an object. It is unpredictable and slow, was deprecated in Java 9 and marked for removal in Java 18, so resources should be released with try-with-resources (AutoCloseable) or a java.lang.ref.Cleaner instead.

common_mistakes: Presenting finalize() as the right way to release resources | Saying a final reference makes the object immutable | Saying finally does not run when try contains a return

question: What is the difference between checked and unchecked exceptions? Give examples of each.
model_answer: Checked exceptions are subclasses of Exception that are not RuntimeException subclasses. The compiler forces you to handle them with try-catch or declare them with a throws clause, because they represent recoverable conditions outside the program's control, such as IOException, FileNotFoundException and SQLException. Unchecked exceptions are RuntimeException and its subclasses; the compiler does not force handling because they usually signal programming bugs, such as NullPointerException, ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, IllegalArgumentException and ArithmeticException. Errors such as OutOfMemoryError are also unchecked but should not normally be caught. The distinction is enforced only at compile time; at runtime both kinds are thrown and propagate the same way.

expected_answer_points: Checked: the compiler forces handling with try-catch or a throws clause | Checked examples: IOException, SQLException | Unchecked: RuntimeException and its subclasses, not enforced by the compiler | Unchecked examples: NullPointerException, IllegalArgumentException | Checked for recoverable external problems; unchecked for programming bugs | Errors such as OutOfMemoryError are unchecked and normally not caught
common_mistakes: Saying checked exceptions happen at compile time and unchecked ones at runtime | Classifying Exception itself as unchecked | Catching Exception or Throwable everywhere

question: A method that calculates a cart total throws NullPointerException at the line `int qty = stock.get(item);`, where stock is a Map<String, Integer> that is definitely not null. What is the cause and how do you fix it?
model_answer: Map.get() returns null when the key is missing. Assigning that Integer to an int triggers auto-unboxing, which calls intValue() on null and throws NullPointerException. Since Java 14 the helpful NullPointerException message says exactly this: Cannot invoke "java.lang.Integer.intValue()" because the return value of "java.util.Map.get(Object)" is null. Fixes: use int qty = stock.getOrDefault(item, 0); if a missing item means zero stock, keep the value as Integer and add a null check if absence needs special handling, or throw a clear exception if a missing key is a real error. In general, read the NPE message, find which reference is null, and fix the source of the null (validation, defaults, Optional) instead of catching NullPointerException.
keywords: Map.get returns null, auto-unboxing, intValue, helpful NullPointerException, getOrDefault, null check, missing key

model_answer: It prints "finally x = 2" followed by "returned 1". When return x executes, the expression is evaluated and the return value 1 is saved; then the finally block always runs before the method actually returns. Changing the local primitive x inside finally does not alter the value that was already saved, so the caller receives 1. The "finally" line appears first because test() must finish, including its finally block, before main can build and print its string. If the finally block had its own return statement, that return would replace the try's value and would also swallow any exception thrown in try, which is why returning from finally is considered bad practice.

model_answer: == on objects is a reference comparison: it checks whether both variables point to the same object, not whether they contain the same characters. The literal "ADMIN" lives in the string pool, but a string read at runtime from a Scanner, a file or a request is a new String object, so == is false even when the text matches. Use a content comparison with equals(): if ("ADMIN".equals(role)). Putting the literal first also avoids a NullPointerException when role is null (Objects.equals(role, "ADMIN") works too). Use equalsIgnoreCase() if the case should not matter, and consider trimming input. == only seemed to work in quick tests where both sides were compile-time literals from the pool.

question: Why are String objects immutable in Java, and what is the String pool?
model_answer: A String's content can never change after creation; methods like toUpperCase() or concat() return a new String. The String pool is an area of the heap where the JVM keeps one shared copy of each string literal, so "java" written in many places refers to the same object. new String("java") deliberately creates a separate object, and intern() returns the pooled copy. Immutability is what makes this sharing safe, because no caller can change a string that others are using. It also makes strings thread-safe without locking, allows hashCode caching (useful for HashMap keys) and gives security, since a validated file path, URL or class name cannot be altered afterwards. The trade-off is that repeated modification creates many objects, which is why StringBuilder exists.

expected_answer_points: String content cannot change; methods return new strings | The String pool keeps one shared copy of each literal on the heap | new String() creates a separate object; intern() returns the pooled copy | Immutability makes pooling and sharing safe | Benefits: thread safety, hashCode caching for map keys, security | Trade-off: many objects on repeated modification, so use StringBuilder
common_mistakes: Thinking s.toUpperCase() changes s | Saying the pool is on the stack or in PermGen (it is on the heap since Java 7) | Saying a final variable is what makes a String immutable

question: What is the difference between String, StringBuilder and StringBuffer, and which would you use to build a large report inside a loop?
model_answer: String is immutable: every modification creates a new object, so concatenating with + or += inside a loop copies the growing text again and again, which is O(n²) for large output. StringBuilder is mutable: append(), insert() and reverse() change an internal resizable buffer in place, and it is not synchronized, so it gives the best performance in single-threaded code. StringBuffer has the same API but synchronized methods, making it thread-safe but slower; it is a legacy class that is rarely needed today. To build a large report in a loop, use one StringBuilder (optionally with an initial capacity) and call toString() once at the end. A simple one-line concatenation like "Hi " + name is fine because the compiler already optimises it.

question: What is the difference between List, Set and Map in the Java Collections Framework? Give one implementation of each.
model_answer: A List is an ordered collection that allows duplicates and access by index, for example ArrayList or LinkedList. A Set stores only unique elements, with duplicates detected through equals() and hashCode(): HashSet has no guaranteed order, LinkedHashSet keeps insertion order and TreeSet keeps elements sorted. A Map stores key-value pairs with unique keys (values may repeat), for example HashMap, LinkedHashMap or TreeMap. List and Set extend the Collection interface, but Map does not. Use a List for an ordered sequence, a Set for uniqueness checks and a Map for fast lookup by key. Since Java 9, List.of(), Set.of() and Map.of() create unmodifiable collections.

question: What is the difference between ArrayList and LinkedList, and which would you choose by default?
model_answer: ArrayList is backed by a resizable (dynamic) array, so get(i) is fast random access in O(1) and adding at the end is amortised O(1); when the array is full it grows by about 50% and copies the elements. Inserting or removing in the middle is O(n) because later elements must shift. LinkedList is a doubly linked list: get(i) is O(n) because it walks node by node, adding or removing at either end is O(1), and a middle insert is O(1) only once you are already at the position, for example through an iterator. Every node stores two extra references, so LinkedList has more memory overhead and poor CPU cache locality. ArrayList is the default choice in almost all cases, and ArrayDeque is usually better than LinkedList for queue or stack usage.

question: Explain how HashMap works internally when you call put(key, value) and get(key). Cover collisions, resizing, and what happens in Java 8+ when one bucket gets too many entries.
model_answer: A HashMap stores entries in an array of buckets (16 by default). On put, it calls key.hashCode(), mixes the high bits into the low bits, and computes the bucket index as hash & (capacity - 1). If the bucket is empty the entry goes there; otherwise it walks the entries in that bucket and uses equals() to look for the same key, replacing its value if found or adding a new node if not (a collision). get repeats the same hash and index calculation and then uses equals() to find the key, so both operations are O(1) on average. When the number of entries exceeds capacity x load factor (0.75), the map resizes: the table doubles and entries are redistributed. Since Java 8, when a bucket grows beyond 8 entries and the table has at least 64 buckets, that bucket becomes a red-black tree, so the worst case is O(log n) instead of O(n). HashMap allows one null key, is not thread-safe, and keys should be immutable, with consistent equals() and hashCode().

question: What is the difference between Comparable and Comparator? How would you sort a list of Employee objects by salary (highest first) and then by name?
model_answer:
Comparable (java.lang) defines a class's natural ordering through compareTo(T other), implemented inside the class itself, so a class has only one natural order; String and Integer implement it. Comparator (java.util) defines an external ordering through compare(a, b), so you can create many different orderings without touching the class. Since Java 8 Comparator has factory and chaining methods:

employees.sort(Comparator.comparingInt(Employee::getSalary).reversed()
    .thenComparing(Employee::getName));

Collections.sort(list) and TreeSet use the natural ordering by default and accept a Comparator to override it. Both methods must return a negative number, zero or a positive number; use Integer.compare() rather than subtraction to avoid integer overflow.

question: What problem do generics solve, what is type erasure, and when would you use `List<? extends Number>` versus `List<? super Integer>`?
model_answer: Generics give compile-time type safety and remove explicit casts: a List<String> can only hold strings, so mistakes are caught by the compiler instead of appearing as ClassCastException at runtime. They also allow reusable code, such as a bounded type parameter in <T extends Comparable<T>> T max(List<T> list). Type erasure means generic types are checked only at compile time and erased from the bytecode (List<String> becomes a plain List at runtime), so you cannot write new T(), use primitives as type arguments or test whether an Object is a List<String>. Wildcards follow PECS, Producer Extends, Consumer Super. List<? extends Number> is a producer: you can read Numbers from it but cannot add elements (except null), so a sum(List<? extends Number>) method accepts both List<Integer> and List<Double>. List<? super Integer> is a consumer: you can safely add Integers to it, so a fill method accepts List<Integer>, List<Number> or List<Object>.
keywords: compile-time type safety, explicit casts, ClassCastException, bounded type parameter, type erasure, wildcard, PECS, producer extends, consumer super

question: How do you create and start a thread in Java? What goes wrong if you call run() instead of start()?
model_answer: You can extend Thread and override run(), or, preferably, implement Runnable (or Callable<V> when the task returns a result or throws a checked exception) and pass it to a Thread or an ExecutorService. Runnable is preferred because it separates the task from the thread that runs it and leaves your class free to extend another class. Runnable is a functional interface, so a lambda works: new Thread(() -> System.out.println("working")).start(); Calling start() asks the JVM to create a new thread with its own new call stack, and that thread then calls run(). Calling run() directly is just a normal method call on the current thread, so nothing runs concurrently. Calling start() twice on the same Thread object throws IllegalThreadStateException.

question: An order service starts a new Thread for every order to send a confirmation email. During a sale it crashes with `OutOfMemoryError: unable to create native thread`. What is wrong with the design and how would you redesign it?
model_answer: Creating one platform thread per task is unbounded: every thread reserves its own stack memory and an operating-system thread, so thousands of simultaneous orders exhaust memory or the OS thread limit, and creating and context-switching so many threads also wastes CPU. I would use an ExecutorService thread pool instead. A ThreadPoolExecutor with a fixed number of worker threads, a bounded queue and a rejection policy reuses threads, queues extra work and applies back-pressure instead of crashing (Executors.newFixedThreadPool is simpler but its queue is unbounded). Tasks are submitted with executor.submit(task) or CompletableFuture.runAsync(task, executor). Failures must be handled and logged, with retries, because an exception inside a submitted task is otherwise hidden in its Future, and on application stop the pool is closed with shutdown() and awaitTermination(). The pool size fits the workload: I/O-bound email sending can use more threads than CPU cores, within the mail server's rate limit. On Java 21+, virtual threads (Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) make a thread per blocking task cheap, but the rate limit still applies. For durability, a message queue can hold emails if the service restarts.
keywords: unbounded threads, thread pool, ExecutorService, reuses threads, bounded queue, rejection policy, shutdown, CompletableFuture, virtual threads

common_mistakes: Increasing the heap size or the OS thread limit | Switching to Executors.newCachedThreadPool, which can also create unbounded threads | Forgetting to shut the executor down

question: What is a lambda expression in Java, and how is it related to a functional interface?
model_answer: A lambda expression, added in Java 8, is a short way to write an anonymous function: a parameter list, an arrow and a body, for example (a, b) -> a + b. A lambda has no type of its own; it is always converted to a functional interface, an interface with a single abstract method (it may still have default and static methods), optionally marked with @FunctionalInterface so the compiler checks it. The lambda becomes the implementation of that one method. Common built-in functional interfaces in java.util.function are Predicate<T> (test, returns boolean), Function<T, R> (apply), Consumer<T> (accept) and Supplier<T> (get). A lambda can use local variables from the enclosing method only if they are effectively final, and a method reference such as String::toUpperCase is a shorter form of a lambda.

question: Given `record Employee(String name, String dept, int salary)` and a List<Employee> employees, write a stream pipeline that returns the names of employees in the "IT" department earning more than 50,000, highest salary first. Then compute the average salary per department.
model_answer:
List<String> topIt = employees.stream()
    .filter(e -> e.dept().equals("IT"))
    .filter(e -> e.salary() > 50_000)
    .sorted(Comparator.comparingInt(Employee::salary).reversed())
    .map(Employee::name)
    .toList();

Map<String, Double> avgByDept = employees.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Employee::dept,
        Collectors.averagingInt(Employee::salary)));

filter keeps only the matching employees, sorted orders them with a Comparator (reversed for highest first), and map turns each Employee into its name. These are lazy intermediate operations; toList() (Java 16+, returning an unmodifiable list) is the terminal operation that runs the pipeline, and collect(Collectors.toList()) is the older equivalent. groupingBy builds a Map keyed by department with averagingInt as the downstream collector. Sorting happens before map because the salary is no longer available after mapping to names, and the source list is not modified.

It prints:

Intermediate operations such as filter and map use lazy evaluation: building the pipeline runs nothing, so "pipeline built" is printed first. Elements then flow element by element through the whole pipeline rather than stage by stage: 1 fails the filter, 2 passes and is immediately mapped to 20. findFirst is short-circuiting, so the stream stops there and 3 to 6 are never examined. Calling s.findFirst() again would throw IllegalStateException, because a stream can be consumed only once.

question: What is a record in Java (Java 16+), and when would you use one instead of a normal class?
model_answer: A record is a compact class that acts as a transparent carrier for immutable data. Writing record Point(int x, int y) {} automatically gives private final fields, a canonical constructor, accessor methods x() and y() (not getX()), and equals(), hashCode() and toString() based on all components. Records are implicitly final, cannot extend another class (they already extend java.lang.Record) but can implement interfaces, and cannot declare extra instance fields; they may add static members, methods and a compact constructor for validation, such as rejecting a negative value. Use records for DTOs, API responses, method results and map keys. Use a normal class when you need mutable state, inheritance or hidden internal fields.

question: What is Inversion of Control (IoC) in Spring, and what is the IoC container?
model_answer: Inversion of Control is a design principle in which the framework, not your own code, creates objects and wires their dependencies. In Spring the IoC container is represented by the ApplicationContext interface, which extends BeanFactory. It reads the configuration (stereotype annotations such as @Component, @Bean methods in @Configuration classes), instantiates the beans, injects their dependencies and manages the bean lifecycle. Classes only declare what they need, which gives loose coupling and makes them easy to unit test with mocks. Dependency injection is the technique Spring uses to implement IoC.

common_mistakes: Saying IoC and dependency injection are unrelated concepts | Thinking the developer still calls new for every Spring-managed object | Confusing the IoC container with the embedded web server

question: Spring supports constructor injection, setter injection and field injection. How do they differ, and which one is recommended for mandatory dependencies?
model_answer: Constructor injection passes dependencies through the constructor. The fields can be final (supporting immutability), the object is never half-initialised, a missing dependency fails at startup, and the class can be unit tested with plain new and mocks. Since Spring 4.3 a class with a single constructor needs no @Autowired. Setter injection calls @Autowired setter methods after construction; it suits optional dependencies or ones that may be changed later, but the object can exist without them. Field injection puts @Autowired directly on private fields; it is short but hides the dependencies, prevents final fields and makes the class hard to test without Spring or reflection. Constructor injection is the recommended style for mandatory dependencies.

question: After a refactor, startup fails with 'The dependencies of some of the beans in the application context form a cycle', listing orderService -> invoiceService -> orderService. Both services use constructor injection. Why does Spring Boot refuse to start, and how should you fix it?
model_answer: OrderService needs InvoiceService in its constructor and InvoiceService needs OrderService in its constructor, so neither bean can be created first. With constructor injection Spring cannot hand out a half-built early reference, so the cycle can never be resolved (internally a BeanCurrentlyInCreationException). In addition, since Spring Boot 2.6 circular references are prohibited by default (spring.main.allow-circular-references=false), so even field or setter injection cycles fail fast. A circular dependency usually signals a design problem, so the proper fix is to restructure: extract the shared logic into a third service (for example BillingService) that both depend on, or decouple the calls with application events so one service publishes an event instead of calling the other. As a short-term workaround, @Lazy on one constructor parameter injects a proxy and resolves the real bean on first use. Setting allow-circular-references=true does not help constructor cycles at all and only hides the design problem.
keywords: circular dependency, constructor injection, BeanCurrentlyInCreationException, allow-circular-references, @Lazy, third service, application events
expected_answer_points: Each bean needs the other in its constructor, so neither can be created first | Constructor-injection cycles cannot be resolved (BeanCurrentlyInCreationException) | Spring Boot 2.6+ prohibits circular references by default | Proper fix is a redesign, such as extracting shared logic into a third service | Another option is decoupling with application events | @Lazy on one parameter is only a workaround

question: What is a Spring bean, and what bean scopes does Spring provide?
model_answer: A Spring bean is an object whose creation, dependency wiring and lifecycle are managed by the Spring IoC container. Beans are declared with stereotype annotations such as @Component or @Service that component scanning picks up, or with @Bean methods in a @Configuration class. The default scope is singleton: one shared instance per application context. Prototype creates a new instance every time the bean is requested from the container. Web applications also have request scope (one instance per HTTP request), session scope (one per HTTP session) and application scope (one per ServletContext). The scope is changed with @Scope, for example @Scope("prototype").
keywords: IoC container, singleton, prototype, request scope, session scope, @Scope, component scanning
expected_answer_points: A bean is an object managed by the Spring IoC container | Beans are declared with stereotype annotations or @Bean methods | Default scope is singleton, one instance per application context | Prototype creates a new instance each time it is requested | Web scopes: request, session and application | Scope is changed with @Scope
common_mistakes: Thinking every Java object in the project is a bean | Assuming singleton scope makes a bean thread-safe | Believing the default scope is prototype

Average: correct definition with only singleton and prototype. Weak: describes a bean as any Java object or cannot name scopes.

question: What is the difference between @Component, @Service, @Repository and @Controller?
model_answer: All four are stereotype annotations that mark a class as a Spring bean detected by component scanning; @Service, @Repository and @Controller are specialisations of @Component. @Component is the generic stereotype for any Spring-managed class. @Service marks the business logic layer; it adds no extra behaviour but documents intent. @Repository marks the data access layer and enables persistence exception translation, converting database-specific exceptions into Spring's DataAccessException hierarchy. @Controller marks a Spring MVC controller in the web layer whose methods handle HTTP requests; @RestController combines it with @ResponseBody for REST APIs. Using the right annotation makes the layered design clear.
keywords: stereotype, component scanning, business logic, exception translation, DataAccessException, data access layer, web layer
expected_answer_points: All are stereotype annotations detected by component scanning | @Service, @Repository and @Controller are specialisations of @Component | @Service marks business logic and adds no extra behaviour | @Repository adds persistence exception translation to DataAccessException | @Controller handles HTTP requests in the web layer

question: What is the difference between the Spring Framework and Spring Boot?
model_answer: The Spring Framework provides the core features: the IoC container, dependency injection, Spring MVC, data access, transactions and AOP. With plain Spring you choose compatible library versions yourself and configure things like the DispatcherServlet, data source and web server manually. Spring Boot is built on top of Spring and gets an application running with minimal setup: auto-configuration creates sensible default beans based on the classpath, starter dependencies bring compatible libraries together, and an embedded server (Tomcat by default) lets you run the app as an executable JAR with java -jar. The optional Actuator starter adds health checks and metrics. Spring Boot does not replace Spring; it removes boilerplate configuration.
keywords: IoC container, auto-configuration, starter dependencies, embedded server, executable JAR, boilerplate configuration, Actuator

question: What does @SpringBootApplication do, and how does Spring Boot's auto-configuration decide which beans to create?
model_answer: @SpringBootApplication combines three annotations: @SpringBootConfiguration (a specialised @Configuration), @EnableAutoConfiguration and @ComponentScan, which scans the main class's package and its sub-packages. For auto-configuration, Spring Boot 3 loads the auto-configuration classes listed in META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports inside its JARs. Each class is guarded by conditions such as @ConditionalOnClass (a library is on the classpath), @ConditionalOnMissingBean (you have not defined your own bean) and @ConditionalOnProperty. So adding spring-boot-starter-data-jpa and a MySQL driver creates a DataSource, EntityManagerFactory and transaction manager automatically, while defining your own bean of that type makes the default back off. Starting the app with --debug prints the conditions evaluation report showing what matched and why.
keywords: @SpringBootConfiguration, @EnableAutoConfiguration, @ComponentScan, @ConditionalOnClass, @ConditionalOnMissingBean, classpath, AutoConfiguration.imports, conditions evaluation report
expected_answer_points: @SpringBootApplication = @SpringBootConfiguration + @EnableAutoConfiguration + @ComponentScan | Component scanning covers the main class's package and sub-packages | Auto-configuration classes are listed in AutoConfiguration.imports | Conditions such as @ConditionalOnClass and @ConditionalOnMissingBean decide what is created | Beans you define yourself make the auto-configured defaults back off | --debug prints the conditions evaluation report
common_mistakes: Saying Spring Boot 3 registers auto-configuration in spring.factories | Thinking auto-configuration overrides beans the developer defined | Believing @ComponentScan scans the whole classpath
follow_up_question: How would you exclude one auto-configuration, for example DataSourceAutoConfiguration?

Average: knows the three annotations but describes auto-configuration vaguely. Weak: says it simply 'configures everything automatically' with no mechanism.

question: What are Spring Boot starters? Which starters would a typical REST API backed by MySQL use?
model_answer: A starter is a dependency descriptor that pulls in a tested, compatible set of libraries for one feature, so you add one dependency instead of many, and versions are managed by the Spring Boot parent POM or BOM. A REST API with MySQL typically uses spring-boot-starter-web (Spring MVC, Jackson and embedded Tomcat), spring-boot-starter-data-jpa (Spring Data JPA with Hibernate), spring-boot-starter-validation (Hibernate Validator for Jakarta Bean Validation), the mysql-connector-j JDBC driver, spring-boot-starter-security for authentication, and spring-boot-starter-test (JUnit 5, Mockito, AssertJ) for tests. Adding a starter also activates the matching auto-configuration.

expected_answer_points: A starter is a dependency descriptor bundling compatible libraries for a feature | Versions are managed by the Spring Boot parent or BOM | spring-boot-starter-web brings Spring MVC, Jackson and embedded Tomcat | spring-boot-starter-data-jpa brings Spring Data JPA with Hibernate | spring-boot-starter-validation plus the mysql-connector-j driver | Starters activate the related auto-configuration

question: Your main class is com.app.StoreApplication. You add ProductController in the package com.controller with @RestController and @GetMapping("/api/products"). The app starts without errors, but GET /api/products returns 404. What is wrong and how do you fix it?
model_answer: @SpringBootApplication triggers component scanning only in the package of the main class (com.app) and its sub-packages. com.controller is a sibling package, so ProductController is never registered as a bean and no handler mapping exists for /api/products. Startup succeeds because nothing depends on the controller, and the request simply falls through to a 404. The clean fix is the standard package structure: keep the main class in the root (base package) and put every layer beneath it, such as com.app.controller, com.app.service, com.app.repository, com.app.entity and com.app.dto. Alternatively use @SpringBootApplication(scanBasePackages = {"com.app", "com.controller"}), but moving the package is preferred; JPA entities and repositories outside the root would also need @EntityScan and @EnableJpaRepositories. Other 404 causes worth checking are a server.servlet.context-path prefix or a typo in the mapping.
keywords: component scanning, base package, sub-packages, handler mapping, scanBasePackages, package structure, @SpringBootApplication
expected_answer_points: Component scanning starts at the main class's package and covers only sub-packages | com.controller is outside com.app, so the controller is never registered | No handler mapping exists, so the request returns 404 although startup succeeds | Fix: keep the main class in the root package with layers in sub-packages | Alternative: scanBasePackages, plus @EntityScan/@EnableJpaRepositories for JPA types
common_mistakes: Assuming Spring scans every package on the classpath | Adding @ComponentScan on the controller class itself | Only checking the URL and ignoring the package location

evaluation_notes: Strong: explains that scanning starts at the main class package, why startup still succeeds, and fixes it by restructuring packages (mentioning scanBasePackages as an alternative). Average: suggests moving the class without explaining scanning. Weak: blames the URL or HTTP method only.

question: How do you connect a Spring Boot application to a MySQL database? Show the key application.properties entries and explain what spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto controls.
model_answer:
Add spring-boot-starter-data-jpa and the mysql-connector-j driver, then configure the datasource. Spring Boot auto-configures a HikariCP connection pool, the EntityManagerFactory and a transaction manager; the driver class is detected from the URL.

spring.datasource.url=jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/shopdb
spring.datasource.username=shop_user
spring.datasource.password=${DB_PASSWORD}
spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=validate
spring.jpa.show-sql=true

ddl-auto controls Hibernate schema generation at startup: create (drop and recreate tables), create-drop (also drop on shutdown), update (alter tables to match entities), validate (only check that tables match the entities) and none. update is convenient in development, but production should use validate or none with a migration tool such as Flyway or Liquibase. The password should come from an environment variable, not be hard-coded, and show-sql is for development only.
keywords: spring.datasource.url, mysql-connector-j, HikariCP, schema generation, validate, Flyway, environment variable
expected_answer_points: Add spring-boot-starter-data-jpa and the mysql-connector-j driver | Set spring.datasource.url, username and password | Spring Boot auto-configures HikariCP, the EntityManagerFactory and a transaction manager | ddl-auto options: create, create-drop, update, validate, none | Use validate or none with Flyway or Liquibase in production | Keep credentials in environment variables
common_mistakes: Using ddl-auto=create in production and losing data on restart | Hard-coding the production password in application.properties | Using the old com.mysql.jdbc.Driver class name

question: In development your app should use a local MySQL database with SQL logging on, while in production it must use a cloud MySQL server whose credentials are not stored in the code repository. How would you set this up in Spring Boot?
model_answer: Use Spring profiles. Keep shared settings in application.properties and create application-dev.properties (local URL, spring.jpa.show-sql=true, ddl-auto=update) and application-prod.properties (production URL, ddl-auto=validate, quieter logging). Profile-specific files override the default file. Activate a profile with spring.profiles.active=dev on a developer machine, and in production with the environment variable SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod or the command-line argument --spring.profiles.active=prod. Production secrets are supplied as environment variables, either directly (SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD) or through a placeholder such as ${DB_PASSWORD}; because of property precedence, environment variables and command-line arguments override values in property files. Beans that should exist only in one environment, such as a fake email sender, are annotated with @Profile("dev").
keywords: application-dev.properties, application-prod.properties, spring.profiles.active, SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE, environment variables, property precedence, @Profile

Average: knows profile files and spring.profiles.active but not how secrets are supplied. Weak: suggests editing the file before each deployment.

question: What is the difference between @Controller and @RestController?
model_answer: @Controller marks a Spring MVC controller whose handler methods normally return a view name that a template engine such as Thymeleaf renders into HTML; to return data instead, each method needs @ResponseBody. @RestController is a convenience annotation that combines @Controller and @ResponseBody, so every method's return value is written directly to the HTTP response body. An HttpMessageConverter (Jackson for JSON) serializes the returned object based on the request's Accept header. Use @RestController for REST APIs consumed by a React or mobile front end, and @Controller for server-rendered pages.

expected_answer_points: @Controller methods usually return view names rendered by a template engine | @RestController = @Controller + @ResponseBody | Return values are written straight to the response body | HttpMessageConverter with Jackson converts objects to JSON | @RestController for REST APIs, @Controller for server-rendered pages

question: Explain the difference between @PathVariable, @RequestParam and @RequestBody, with an example of when to use each.
model_answer: @PathVariable binds a value from the URI template and identifies a specific resource: @GetMapping("/users/{id}") with @PathVariable Long id handles /users/42. @RequestParam binds a query parameter from the query string (or a form field) and suits optional inputs such as filtering and paging: /users?role=ADMIN&page=0 with @RequestParam(defaultValue = "0") int page. A @RequestParam is required by default unless required = false or a defaultValue is given. @RequestBody deserializes the HTTP request body, usually JSON, into a Java object (typically a DTO) using Jackson, and is used for POST, PUT and PATCH payloads such as creating a user. One handler method can combine all three.
keywords: URI template, query parameter, filtering and paging, required by default, request body, Jackson, DTO

question: A teammate's GET /api/users/{id} endpoint returns the User JPA entity directly. The response contains the password hash, and because User has a bidirectional orders list, serialization either recurses endlessly or fails with a lazy-loading error. What is going wrong, and how would you redesign it?
model_answer: Returning entities couples the API to the database model. Jackson serializes every getter, so sensitive data such as the password hash leaks. The bidirectional User-Order mapping makes Jackson follow user -> orders -> user in an infinite recursion, and touching the lazy orders collection after the persistence context has closed throws LazyInitializationException (or fires extra queries if open-in-view is on). The fix is DTOs: a UserResponse record with only the fields the client needs (id, name, email, order count) and a separate UserRequest DTO with validation for input. The service maps entity to DTO inside the transaction, manually or with MapStruct, and the controller returns only DTOs. This decouples the API contract from the entity, so the database model can change without breaking clients. @JsonIgnore or @JsonManagedReference and @JsonBackReference can stop the recursion, but they are patches, not a design.
keywords: sensitive data, infinite recursion, LazyInitializationException, response DTO, entity-to-DTO mapping, MapStruct, API contract, @JsonIgnore
expected_answer_points: Returning entities exposes sensitive fields such as the password hash | Bidirectional relationships cause infinite recursion during JSON serialization | Lazy collections throw LazyInitializationException or trigger extra queries | Use separate request and response DTOs containing only the needed fields | Map entity to DTO in the service layer, manually or with MapStruct | DTOs decouple the API contract from the database model
common_mistakes: Only adding @JsonIgnore to the password and still returning entities | Switching the relationship to EAGER to hide the lazy-loading error | Doing the DTO mapping inside the repository layer
follow_up_question: Where exactly would you do the entity-to-DTO mapping, and why there?

Average: suggests DTOs but explains only one problem. Weak: suggests @JsonIgnore everywhere or EAGER fetching as the solution.

question: A DTO has @NotBlank on its name field, yet requests with an empty name are saved to the database without any error. The controller method is: public UserDto create(@RequestBody UserDto dto). What are the likely causes?

Fix: public UserDto create(@Valid @RequestBody UserDto dto). A second common cause is that spring-boot-starter-validation is not on the classpath: since Spring Boot 2.3 the web starter no longer brings a validation provider (Hibernate Validator), so the annotations compile but nothing enforces them. Also check that the annotations are imported from jakarta.validation.constraints, because javax.validation annotations are ignored in Spring Boot 3, and that nested objects are marked with @Valid so cascaded validation reaches them.

question: Explain the controller-service-repository layered architecture of a Spring Boot application. What belongs in each layer, and what should each layer not do?
model_answer:
A request flows Controller -> Service -> Repository -> database, with DTOs crossing the web boundary and entities staying inside the application.
- Controller layer (@RestController): handles HTTP only. It maps URLs, reads path, query and body input, triggers @Valid validation, calls a service and returns DTOs with status codes. It should not contain business rules or call repositories directly.
- Service layer (@Service): holds business logic and use cases, coordinates several repositories, defines @Transactional boundaries and maps entities to DTOs. It should not depend on HTTP types such as HttpServletRequest or ResponseEntity.
- Repository layer (Spring Data JPA interfaces): data access only, meaning CRUD and queries on entities. It should not make business decisions.
- Supporting packages: entity, dto, exception (with a @RestControllerAdvice), config and security.
Dependencies point only downward and are wired with constructor injection. Benefits: separation of concerns, easier unit testing of each layer with mocks of the layer below (Mockito, @WebMvcTest, @DataJpaTest), and changes such as a new database or API format stay local to one layer.
keywords: separation of concerns, controller layer, service layer, repository layer, business logic, @Transactional, DTO, unit testing
expected_answer_points: Controller handles HTTP, validation and status codes only | Service holds business logic and transaction boundaries | Repository handles data access only | DTOs at the API boundary, entities inside | Dependencies flow downward via constructor injection | Benefits: separation of concerns and unit testing with mocks
common_mistakes: Putting business logic or repository calls in controllers | Returning ResponseEntity or using HTTP objects in the service layer | Placing @Transactional on controllers

Average: names the layers with brief roles but no boundaries. Weak: cannot explain why the layers are separated.

question: Design the Spring Boot backend for a 'place order' feature: the request has a customer id and a list of product ids with quantities; the system must check stock, save the order with its items, reduce stock and send a confirmation email. Describe the classes in each layer, where the transaction boundary goes, and how you handle failures.
model_answer:
Web layer: OrderController exposes POST /api/orders, accepts a PlaceOrderRequest DTO validated with @Valid (@NotEmpty items, @Positive quantity) and returns 201 with an OrderResponse DTO.
Service layer: OrderService.placeOrder(request) is annotated @Transactional. In one transaction it loads the customer and products, checks stock, creates the Order entity with its OrderItem children, decreases each product's stock and saves the order. A missing product or insufficient stock throws a custom exception that extends RuntimeException (ResourceNotFoundException, InsufficientStockException), so the whole transaction rolls back and no partial order or stock change is kept.
Data layer: OrderRepository, ProductRepository and CustomerRepository extend JpaRepository. Order maps items with @OneToMany(mappedBy = "order", cascade = CascadeType.ALL), so saving the order saves its items. Product has a @Version field for optimistic locking, so two concurrent orders cannot oversell the same stock; the loser gets ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException.

question: What is the difference between JPA, Hibernate and Spring Data JPA?
model_answer: JPA (Jakarta Persistence API) is a specification: a set of interfaces and annotations in jakarta.persistence, such as @Entity and EntityManager, that define how Java objects are mapped to relational tables. It has no implementation of its own. Hibernate is an ORM framework and the most widely used JPA implementation; it is the default persistence provider in Spring Boot, generates the SQL and manages the persistence context. Spring Data JPA is a Spring abstraction on top of JPA that removes boilerplate data-access code: you declare repository interfaces such as JpaRepository, and Spring generates implementations for CRUD, paging and derived queries at runtime, using the EntityManager and Hibernate underneath.
keywords: specification, Jakarta Persistence, ORM, persistence provider, EntityManager, JpaRepository, boilerplate

common_mistakes: Calling JPA a framework that can run on its own | Thinking Spring Data JPA replaces Hibernate | Using javax.persistence in a Spring Boot 3 project

question: Inside a @Transactional service method, a developer loads a Product with findById, calls product.setPrice(499) and never calls save(). The new price still appears in the database. Why, and in which situations would the change not be saved?
model_answer: An entity loaded inside a transaction is a managed entity: it lives in the Hibernate persistence context, the first-level cache of the EntityManager. At flush time, which happens before the transaction commits (and before some queries), Hibernate performs dirty checking: it compares every managed entity with the snapshot taken when it was loaded and issues an UPDATE for changed fields. So save() is not needed for managed entities; it matters for new entities (persist) and detached ones (merge). The change is not saved when no transaction is active (for example @Transactional on a private or self-invoked method, so nothing commits and flushes), when the transaction is readOnly (Spring switches Hibernate's flush mode to manual), when the transaction rolls back, or when the entity is a detached entity, such as one loaded in an earlier transaction or cleared from the context.
keywords: managed entity, persistence context, first-level cache, dirty checking, flush, commit, detached entity, readOnly
expected_answer_points: Entities loaded in a transaction are managed by the persistence context | Hibernate dirty checking compares entities with their loaded snapshot | Changes are flushed as UPDATE statements before commit | save() is needed for new or detached entities, not managed ones | Not saved if there is no active transaction, it is read-only, it rolls back, or the entity is detached
common_mistakes: Believing save() must always be called to update a row | Thinking the UPDATE runs immediately when the setter is called | Assuming a readOnly transaction still writes changes
follow_up_question: What is the difference between persist and merge, and which one does Spring Data's save() call?

Average: says Hibernate tracks changes automatically but cannot explain flush or the exceptions. Weak: claims it is a bug or that save() is always required.

question: How can a Spring Data JPA repository perform CRUD operations and a query like findByEmail when you only write an interface and never an implementation class?
model_answer: When the interface extends JpaRepository<Student, Long>, Spring Data creates a proxy implementation at startup, backed by SimpleJpaRepository and the EntityManager. It inherits ready-made CRUD and paging methods such as save, findById, findAll (with Sort or Pageable), count, existsById and deleteById. For custom methods Spring parses the method name, so derived query methods like findByEmail(String email) become a JPQL query similar to select s from Student s where s.email = ?1. Keywords such as And, Or, Between, LessThan, Containing and OrderBy are supported, and the return type can be Optional<Student>, List<Student> or Page<Student>. Queries too complex for a method name use @Query with JPQL or native SQL. A method name that refers to a non-existent property fails at startup.

model_answer:
employees is a @OneToMany collection, which is FetchType.LAZY by default, so findById loads only the Department plus an uninitialized collection proxy. The service method has no transaction, so findById runs in the repository's own short transaction; when it returns, the persistence context (Hibernate Session) closes and the Department becomes a detached entity. Calling getEmployees().size() then tries to load the collection with no open Session, and Hibernate throws LazyInitializationException. With open-in-view disabled, nothing keeps the Session open for the web request.
Fixes:
1) Annotate the service method with @Transactional(readOnly = true) so the entity stays managed while the DTO is built.
2) Fetch what you need in the query: @Query("select d from Department d left join fetch d.employees where d.id = :id") or @EntityGraph(attributePaths = "employees") on a repository method.
3) If only the count is needed, use a DTO projection or a countByDepartmentId query in EmployeeRepository.
Do not switch the relationship to EAGER or re-enable open-in-view just to hide the error; both cause extra, hidden queries.

question: GET /api/departments returns 50 departments, each with the names of its employees. With SQL logging on, you see 1 query for the departments followed by 50 separate queries for employees, and the endpoint is slow. What is this problem called, why does it happen, and how would you fix it in Spring Data JPA?
model_answer:
This is the N+1 select problem. findAll() runs one query for the departments; employees is a lazily loaded collection, so when the code or Jackson touches each department's employees, Hibernate runs one more query per department. Switching to EAGER does not fix it, because a findAll query still loads eager collections with separate selects. Fixes:
1) Load the association in the same query with JOIN FETCH, e.g. @Query("select d from Department d left join fetch d.employees"), or @EntityGraph(attributePaths = "employees") on the repository method.
2) Enable batch fetching (@BatchSize or hibernate.default_batch_fetch_size) so collections load with a few IN queries.
3) If only names are needed, query a DTO projection directly.
With pagination, JOIN FETCH on a collection makes Hibernate paginate in memory, so paged endpoints should prefer batch fetching or a two-step query.
keywords: N+1 select problem, lazy loading, JOIN FETCH, @EntityGraph, batch fetching, DTO projection, pagination
expected_answer_points: It is the N+1 select problem: one query plus one per department | Caused by lazily loaded collections accessed in a loop or during serialization | Switching to EAGER does not solve it | Fix with JOIN FETCH or @EntityGraph to load everything in one query | Alternatives: batch fetching or a DTO projection | JOIN FETCH on a collection with pagination paginates in memory
common_mistakes: Setting the relationship to EAGER | Adding a cache instead of fixing the query pattern | Using JOIN FETCH with Pageable without noticing in-memory pagination
follow_up_question: How would you write a test that fails if this endpoint starts issuing N+1 queries again?
evaluation_notes: Strong: names the N+1 problem, explains lazy loading per row, rejects EAGER, and gives JOIN FETCH/@EntityGraph plus batch fetching or projections with the pagination caveat. Average: names the problem and one fix. Weak: suggests EAGER or more hardware.

question: What does @Transactional do in a Spring Boot service, and how does Spring implement it behind the scenes?
model_answer: @Transactional declares that a method (or all methods of a class when placed on the class) runs inside a database transaction: Spring starts or joins a transaction before the method, commits it if the method returns normally and rolls it back if it throws. Spring implements this with AOP: the bean is wrapped in a proxy, and the proxy's TransactionInterceptor asks the PlatformTransactionManager (JpaTransactionManager with Spring Data JPA) to begin, commit or roll back around the real method. By default it rolls back only for unchecked exceptions (RuntimeException and Error), not checked ones, unless rollbackFor is set. Useful attributes are propagation (the default REQUIRED joins an existing transaction), readOnly for queries, isolation and timeout. It belongs on the service layer, where one use case may call several repositories that must succeed or fail together.
keywords: commit, rollback, AOP, proxy, PlatformTransactionManager, unchecked exceptions, propagation, service layer

common_mistakes: Thinking @Transactional rolls back for every exception by default | Believing it works on any method regardless of how it is called | Putting @Transactional on each repository call instead of the whole use case

Average: explains commit/rollback but not the proxy. Weak: says it only 'makes the method safe' without any mechanism.

question: What happens when you add spring-boot-starter-security to a Spring Boot 3 REST API without writing any security configuration, and how does Spring Security authenticate a request?
model_answer: Auto-configuration secures every endpoint: unauthenticated requests are rejected with 401 (browsers are redirected to a login page), form login and HTTP Basic are enabled, CSRF protection is on, and a default user named user is created with a generated random password printed in the console (configurable with spring.security.user.name and spring.security.user.password). Authentication happens in a chain of servlet filters, the SecurityFilterChain, which runs before the DispatcherServlet reaches any controller. A filter such as BasicAuthenticationFilter or UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter extracts the credentials and passes them to the AuthenticationManager, which delegates to an AuthenticationProvider. The provider loads the user with UserDetailsService.loadUserByUsername and checks the password with the PasswordEncoder. On success an Authentication object holding the user and their authorities is stored in the SecurityContextHolder for authorization checks and later code; on failure the request is rejected.
keywords: default user, generated password, servlet filters, SecurityFilterChain, AuthenticationManager, UserDetailsService, PasswordEncoder, SecurityContextHolder

question: What is a relational database, and how does an RDBMS like MySQL organize data?
model_answer: A relational database stores data in tables (relations) made of rows and columns. Each row is one record and each column is an attribute with a fixed data type. Tables are related through keys: a primary key uniquely identifies each row, and a foreign key in one table refers to the primary key of another. An RDBMS such as MySQL is the software that stores these tables, lets you query and change them with SQL, enforces constraints and supports transactions so the data stays consistent.
keywords: tables, rows, columns, primary key, foreign key, relationships, SQL, constraints
expected_answer_points: Data is stored in tables of rows and columns | Each row is a record, each column an attribute with a data type | Relationships between tables are made with primary and foreign keys | An RDBMS manages storage, SQL querying, constraints and transactions

question: What is the difference between DDL, DML, DCL and TCL commands in SQL? Give examples of each.
model_answer: SQL commands are grouped by purpose. DDL (Data Definition Language) defines structure: CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE and RENAME. DML (Data Manipulation Language) works on rows: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, and SELECT, which is sometimes listed separately as DQL. DCL (Data Control Language) manages permissions: GRANT and REVOKE. TCL (Transaction Control Language) manages transactions: START TRANSACTION, COMMIT, ROLLBACK and SAVEPOINT. In MySQL, DDL statements cause an implicit commit, so they cannot be rolled back the way DML changes can.
keywords: DDL, DML, DCL, TCL, CREATE, INSERT, GRANT, COMMIT, implicit commit
expected_answer_points: DDL defines structure: CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE | DML changes data: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE (SELECT as DQL) | DCL controls access: GRANT, REVOKE | TCL controls transactions: COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT | DDL causes an implicit commit in MySQL
common_mistakes: Putting TRUNCATE under DML | Saying a DROP TABLE can be rolled back | Not knowing where SELECT belongs

question: What is a primary key, and what rules must a primary key column follow?
model_answer: A primary key is a column, or a set of columns, that uniquely identifies each row in a table. Its values must be unique and NOT NULL, and a table can have only one primary key, although it may be a composite key made of several columns. In InnoDB the primary key is also the clustered index, so rows are stored in primary key order and lookups by it are fast. A good primary key is short and never changes, which is why an AUTO_INCREMENT integer such as emp_id is common.
keywords: unique, NOT NULL, one per table, composite key, clustered index, AUTO_INCREMENT, identifies each row
expected_answer_points: Uniquely identifies each row | Values must be unique and NOT NULL | Only one primary key per table, but it can be composite | InnoDB uses it as the clustered index | Should be short and stable, for example AUTO_INCREMENT
common_mistakes: Saying a table can have several primary keys | Saying a primary key may contain one NULL | Thinking a primary key is only an index with no uniqueness rule
follow_up_question: When would you choose a natural key such as an email over a surrogate AUTO_INCREMENT key?
evaluation_notes: Strong: unique + NOT NULL, one per table, composite option, clustered index or stability. Average: unique and not null only. Weak: 'the first column of the table' or similar.

question: What is the difference between a PRIMARY KEY and a UNIQUE constraint in MySQL?
model_answer: Both enforce uniqueness and both are backed by an index. A table can have only one PRIMARY KEY but many UNIQUE constraints. Primary key columns are always NOT NULL, while a UNIQUE column can hold NULLs, and MySQL allows multiple NULLs because NULL is never equal to NULL. In InnoDB the primary key is the clustered index that stores the rows, while a UNIQUE constraint creates a secondary index. Use the primary key as the row identifier (emp_id) and UNIQUE for other values that must not repeat, such as an email or dept_name.
keywords: one per table, multiple UNIQUE constraints, NOT NULL, NULL allowed, clustered index, secondary index, row identifier
expected_answer_points: Both enforce uniqueness and create an index | Only one primary key per table; many UNIQUE constraints allowed | Primary key is NOT NULL; UNIQUE allows NULLs (several in MySQL) | Primary key is the clustered index in InnoDB; UNIQUE is a secondary index | Primary key is the row identifier; UNIQUE protects other values like email
common_mistakes: Saying a UNIQUE column cannot hold NULL | Saying a UNIQUE column allows only one NULL (SQL Server behaviour, not MySQL) | Saying a UNIQUE constraint does not create an index

question: What is a foreign key, and what happens to employee rows when their department is deleted under ON DELETE RESTRICT, CASCADE and SET NULL? (employees.dept_id references departments.dept_id)
model_answer: A foreign key is a column in a child table whose value must match a key (normally the primary key) in a parent table, or be NULL. It enforces referential integrity, so an employee cannot point to a department that does not exist. The ON DELETE rule decides what happens when the parent row is deleted: RESTRICT, or NO ACTION which is the default in MySQL, blocks the delete while employees still reference the department; CASCADE deletes those employee rows as well; SET NULL keeps the employees and sets their dept_id to NULL, so dept_id must be nullable. InnoDB needs an index on the foreign key column and creates one automatically if none exists.
keywords: referential integrity, child table, parent table, RESTRICT, CASCADE, SET NULL, nullable, index
expected_answer_points: Foreign key value must exist in the parent table's key or be NULL | Enforces referential integrity | RESTRICT / NO ACTION (the default) blocks deleting a referenced parent | CASCADE deletes the child rows too | SET NULL sets the child column to NULL, so it must be nullable | InnoDB requires an index on the foreign key column
common_mistakes: Thinking CASCADE is the default | Using SET NULL on a NOT NULL column | Believing a foreign key automatically deletes child rows
follow_up_question: Which ON DELETE rule would you choose for orders.customer_id, and why?
evaluation_notes: Strong: referential integrity, correct behaviour of all three rules, default rule and the nullable requirement for SET NULL. Average: defines a foreign key and explains CASCADE only. Weak: confuses foreign key with primary key.

question: Write CREATE TABLE statements for departments(dept_id, dept_name) and employees(emp_id, name, dept_id, salary, hire_date, manager_id) with suitable constraints: primary keys, a unique department name, a positive salary, a default hire date, and foreign keys for dept_id and manager_id.
model_answer:
CREATE TABLE departments (
  dept_id   INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  dept_name VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL UNIQUE
);

CREATE TABLE employees (
  emp_id     INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  name       VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
  dept_id    INT NULL,
  salary     DECIMAL(10,2) NOT NULL CHECK (salary > 0),
  hire_date  DATE NOT NULL DEFAULT (CURRENT_DATE),
  manager_id INT NULL,
  CONSTRAINT fk_emp_dept FOREIGN KEY (dept_id) REFERENCES departments (dept_id),
  CONSTRAINT fk_emp_manager FOREIGN KEY (manager_id) REFERENCES employees (emp_id)
);

departments is created first because employees references it. manager_id is a self-referencing foreign key and is nullable so the top manager can exist. DECIMAL avoids rounding errors for money; CHECK constraints are enforced from MySQL 8.0.16, and an expression default such as (CURRENT_DATE) needs 8.0.13 or later.
keywords: PRIMARY KEY, AUTO_INCREMENT, UNIQUE, NOT NULL, CHECK, DEFAULT, FOREIGN KEY, REFERENCES, DECIMAL, self-referencing
expected_answer_points: Create the parent table (departments) before the child | PRIMARY KEY with AUTO_INCREMENT on the id columns | NOT NULL UNIQUE on dept_name | CHECK (salary > 0) and DECIMAL for money | DEFAULT (CURRENT_DATE) for hire_date | dept_id REFERENCES departments and self-referencing manager_id REFERENCES employees

question: Using employees(emp_id, name, dept_id, salary, hire_date, manager_id), write a query that returns the name, salary and hire_date of employees in departments 10 or 20 whose salary is between 40,000 and 80,000 and whose name starts with 'A'.
model_answer:
SELECT name, salary, hire_date
FROM employees
WHERE dept_id IN (10, 20)
  AND salary BETWEEN 40000 AND 80000
  AND name LIKE 'A%';

The WHERE clause filters rows before they are returned. The IN operator replaces several OR conditions, BETWEEN is an inclusive range (40000 and 80000 both match), and LIKE 'A%' uses the % wildcard to match any characters after A (_ matches exactly one character). The conditions are combined with AND, so a row must satisfy all of them.

question: In what logical order does MySQL process the clauses of a SELECT statement, and why does referencing a column alias in the WHERE clause fail?
model_answer: Logically a query is evaluated as FROM (with JOINs), then WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, DISTINCT, ORDER BY and finally LIMIT. WHERE filters individual rows before the SELECT list is computed, so an alias defined in SELECT, for example salary * 12 AS annual_salary, does not exist yet and MySQL reports an unknown column error. Repeat the expression in WHERE or wrap the query in a derived table. ORDER BY runs after SELECT, so it can use the alias; MySQL also accepts aliases in GROUP BY and HAVING as an extension. The optimizer may execute steps in a different physical order, but the result must match this logical order.
keywords: FROM, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY, LIMIT, logical order, unknown column, derived table
expected_answer_points: Order: FROM/JOIN, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, DISTINCT, ORDER BY, LIMIT | WHERE runs before SELECT, so SELECT aliases are not yet defined | Fix by repeating the expression or using a derived table | ORDER BY can use SELECT aliases | The optimizer may change physical execution but not the logical result
common_mistakes: Saying SELECT runs first because it is written first | Thinking HAVING runs before GROUP BY | Believing aliases cannot be used anywhere in the query
follow_up_question: In which clauses can a window function such as RANK() appear, and why not in WHERE?
evaluation_notes: Strong: correct full order, explains the alias error and gives a fix. Average: roughly correct order without explaining the alias problem. Weak: says the query runs top to bottom as written.

question: From employees(emp_id, name, dept_id, salary, hire_date, manager_id), write queries to (a) get the 5 highest-paid employees, breaking salary ties by name, and (b) show page 3 of the employee list sorted by name with 10 rows per page.
model_answer:
-- (a) top 5 by salary
SELECT emp_id, name, salary
FROM employees
ORDER BY salary DESC, name ASC
LIMIT 5;

-- (b) page 3, 10 rows per page
SELECT emp_id, name, salary
FROM employees
ORDER BY name, emp_id
LIMIT 10 OFFSET 20;

ORDER BY sorts in ascending order by default; DESC reverses it, and the second column is the tie-breaker. LIMIT n OFFSET m skips m rows: page 3 skips (3 - 1) * 10 = 20 rows, and MySQL also accepts LIMIT 20, 10. Adding the unique emp_id to the sort gives a deterministic order, otherwise rows with equal names can move between pages. LIMIT 5 does not return extra employees tied with the 5th salary.
keywords: ORDER BY, DESC, LIMIT, OFFSET, tie-breaker, deterministic order, ascending default
expected_answer_points: ORDER BY salary DESC for highest first | A second sort column as the tie-breaker | LIMIT 5 returns only the first 5 rows | Page 3 = LIMIT 10 OFFSET 20, i.e. (page - 1) * size | A unique sort key keeps pagination deterministic
common_mistakes: Using LIMIT without ORDER BY and expecting a stable order | Computing OFFSET as page * size | Forgetting DESC and returning the lowest salaries
follow_up_question: How would you return everyone tied with the 5th highest salary instead of exactly 5 rows?
evaluation_notes: Strong: both queries correct with DESC, tie-breaker and the right OFFSET, mentions deterministic ordering. Average: correct queries but wrong OFFSET or no tie-breaker. Weak: no ORDER BY or cannot paginate.

question: What is the difference between DELETE, TRUNCATE and DROP in MySQL?
model_answer: DELETE is a DML command that removes rows, optionally filtered by WHERE. It removes rows one by one, fires DELETE triggers and can be rolled back inside a transaction, but it is slow on large tables and does not reset AUTO_INCREMENT. TRUNCATE TABLE is DDL: it removes all rows by recreating the table, is much faster, resets AUTO_INCREMENT, does not fire triggers, causes an implicit commit so it cannot be rolled back, and fails if another table has a foreign key referencing it. DROP TABLE removes the whole table: data, structure, indexes and constraints.
keywords: DML, DDL, WHERE, rollback, AUTO_INCREMENT, implicit commit, triggers, structure
expected_answer_points: DELETE removes selected rows (WHERE), supports rollback, fires triggers | TRUNCATE removes all rows, is DDL, faster, resets AUTO_INCREMENT | TRUNCATE causes an implicit commit, so no rollback | DROP removes the table structure and its data | TRUNCATE fails on a table referenced by a foreign key
common_mistakes: Saying TRUNCATE accepts a WHERE clause | Saying TRUNCATE can be rolled back in MySQL | Saying DELETE resets AUTO_INCREMENT
follow_up_question: You need to empty a 50-million-row log table every night; which command would you use and what must you check first?
evaluation_notes: Strong: DML vs DDL, rollback, AUTO_INCREMENT, triggers and structure removal. Average: explains what each removes but not rollback or AUTO_INCREMENT. Weak: treats TRUNCATE and DROP as the same.

question: What is the difference between COUNT(*), COUNT(manager_id) and COUNT(DISTINCT manager_id) on the employees table?
model_answer: COUNT(*) counts all rows, including rows that contain NULLs. COUNT(manager_id) counts only rows where manager_id is not NULL, so top-level employees are skipped. COUNT(DISTINCT manager_id) counts the number of distinct non-NULL values, i.e. how many different people are managers. The same NULL rule applies to the other aggregate functions: SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX ignore NULLs, so AVG divides only by the non-NULL count. On an empty set COUNT returns 0 while SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX return NULL.
keywords: counts all rows, ignores NULL, non-NULL values, distinct values, aggregate functions, AVG, empty set
expected_answer_points: COUNT(*) counts every row, NULLs included | COUNT(column) counts only non-NULL values | COUNT(DISTINCT column) counts unique non-NULL values | SUM/AVG/MIN/MAX also ignore NULLs | On an empty set COUNT returns 0, the others return NULL
common_mistakes: Saying COUNT(*) skips rows with NULLs | Believing COUNT(1) is faster than COUNT(*) in MySQL | Assuming AVG treats NULL as 0
follow_up_question: If the salaries are 50000, NULL and 70000, what do AVG(salary) and SUM(salary) / COUNT(*) return?
evaluation_notes: Strong: correct NULL behaviour for all three and for other aggregates, plus empty-set results. Average: correct for COUNT(*) and COUNT(column) only. Weak: says all three return the same number.

question: Using employees(emp_id, name, dept_id, salary, hire_date, manager_id), write a query that shows, for each dept_id, the number of employees, the average salary rounded to 2 decimals and the highest salary, with the largest departments first.
model_answer:
SELECT dept_id,
       COUNT(*) AS emp_count,
       ROUND(AVG(salary), 2) AS avg_salary,
       MAX(salary) AS max_salary
FROM employees
GROUP BY dept_id
ORDER BY emp_count DESC;

GROUP BY dept_id produces one result row per group, and the aggregate functions COUNT, AVG and MAX are calculated inside each group. Every non-aggregated column in SELECT (here only dept_id) must appear in GROUP BY. Employees with a NULL dept_id form their own NULL group. ORDER BY can use the alias emp_count because it runs after SELECT.
keywords: GROUP BY, COUNT, AVG, MAX, ROUND, one row per group, non-aggregated column, NULL group
expected_answer_points: GROUP BY dept_id gives one result row per department | COUNT(*), AVG and MAX computed per group | ROUND(AVG(salary), 2) for the formatting | Non-aggregated SELECT columns must be in GROUP BY | ORDER BY the count in descending order
common_mistakes: Adding name to SELECT without grouping by it | Using WHERE instead of GROUP BY to split departments | Sorting by avg_salary instead of the employee count
follow_up_question: How would you show the department name instead of dept_id, including departments that have no employees?
evaluation_notes: Strong: correct grouped query with all three aggregates, rounding and sorting, explains the GROUP BY rule. Average: correct query with one aggregate wrong or unsorted. Weak: no GROUP BY or selects non-grouped columns.

model_answer:
With ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY, which is on by default in MySQL 8.0, every column in SELECT must be in GROUP BY, be inside an aggregate, or be functionally dependent on the grouped columns. name is none of these: a department has many names, so MySQL cannot know which one to return. Older modes silently returned an arbitrary name, often not the top earner. Adding name to GROUP BY changes the meaning, and ANY_VALUE(name) only hides the bug. Join back to a derived table with the per-department maximum instead:

SELECT e.dept_id, e.name, e.salary
FROM employees e
JOIN (SELECT dept_id, MAX(salary) AS max_sal
      FROM employees
      GROUP BY dept_id) m
  ON m.dept_id = e.dept_id AND m.max_sal = e.salary;

This returns every employee tied for the top salary. A window function, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary DESC) = 1, gives the same result.
keywords: ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY, non-aggregated column, functionally dependent, arbitrary value, derived table, join back, ANY_VALUE, window function
expected_answer_points: ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY rejects a non-aggregated column that is not in GROUP BY | name is not functionally dependent on dept_id | Old behaviour returned an arbitrary value, not the top earner's name | Fix: join back to a derived table of MAX(salary) per dept_id | Alternative: RANK() window function; ANY_VALUE only hides the bug | Ties return more than one employee
common_mistakes: Turning ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY off | Adding name to GROUP BY | Assuming MySQL returns the name from the MAX row
follow_up_question: Why is SELECT emp_id, name, salary FROM employees GROUP BY emp_id accepted under ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY?
