Average: correct outline but misses validation per request or the expiry. Weak: thinks the JWT is stored in the database or that it is encrypted secret data.

question: What is the difference between session-based and token-based (JWT) authentication? When would you prefer each?
model_answer: In session-based authentication the server creates a session after login, stores it (in memory, Redis or a database) and gives the browser a session id in a cookie such as JSESSIONID; the browser sends the cookie automatically and the server looks up the session on each request. It is stateful and easy to revoke by deleting the session, but several servers need shared session storage, and cookie-based auth needs CSRF protection. In token-based authentication the server issues a signed JWT and stores nothing; the client sends it in the Authorization header and any server can verify it with the key, which suits REST APIs, mobile clients and horizontal scaling. A JWT cannot easily be revoked before it expires, so access tokens are kept short-lived and renewed with a refresh token. Prefer sessions for a server-rendered or single-server app, and JWTs for stateless APIs used by SPAs, mobile apps or several services.
keywords: stateful, stateless, session id, cookie, JSESSIONID, revoke, horizontal scaling, refresh token
expected_answer_points: Session: the server stores session state and the browser holds a session id cookie | Token: the server issues a signed JWT and stores no session state (stateless) | Sessions are easy to revoke; a JWT stays valid until it expires | JWTs suit horizontal scaling and mobile/SPA clients; sessions need shared storage when scaled | Cookie-based sessions need CSRF protection; tokens sent in a header do not | Short-lived access tokens plus refresh tokens reduce the revocation problem
common_mistakes: Saying JWT is always more secure than sessions | Thinking sessions cannot be used with a React frontend | Claiming a JWT is invalidated simply by deleting it on the server | Mixing up what the cookie holds and what the token holds
follow_up_question: If you store a JWT in an HttpOnly cookie, is the application still stateless, and does it need CSRF protection?
evaluation_notes: Strong: stateful vs stateless, where state lives, revocation vs scaling trade-off, CSRF implication and when to use each. Average: explains the basic difference but no trade-offs. Weak: 'JWT is newer and better' with no mechanism.

question: Your team is deciding where the React app should keep the JWT after login: localStorage, sessionStorage, or a cookie. What are the security trade-offs, and what would you recommend?
model_answer: localStorage persists across tabs and browser restarts, while sessionStorage lasts only for one tab. Both are readable by any JavaScript on the page, so a single XSS bug lets an attacker steal the token and use it from anywhere. They are not sent automatically, so they are not a CSRF risk. An HttpOnly cookie cannot be read by JavaScript, so XSS cannot steal the token itself (although injected script can still send requests while the page is open). Because browsers send cookies automatically, the cookie must be Secure and SameSite (Strict or Lax), and CSRF protection is needed. A common recommendation: keep a short-lived access token (for example 15 minutes) in memory, in React state or a module variable, and a longer-lived refresh token in an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie limited to the refresh endpoint; after a page reload the app calls the refresh endpoint to get a new access token. Whatever you choose, prevent XSS first, because XSS undermines every storage option.
keywords: localStorage, sessionStorage, HttpOnly cookie, XSS, CSRF, SameSite, in memory, refresh token
expected_answer_points: localStorage and sessionStorage are readable by JavaScript, so XSS can steal the token | Web storage is not sent automatically, so it is not a CSRF risk | HttpOnly cookies cannot be read by JavaScript but are sent automatically, so they need Secure, SameSite and CSRF protection | sessionStorage is per tab and cleared when the tab closes; localStorage persists | Recommended: short-lived access token in memory plus refresh token in an HttpOnly Secure SameSite cookie | Preventing XSS matters whatever the storage choice
common_mistakes: Claiming localStorage is safe because it is isolated per domain | Believing HttpOnly cookies make XSS harmless | Forgetting that cookies bring CSRF risk | Storing long-lived tokens with no expiry
follow_up_question: How does a Content-Security-Policy header reduce the risk of token theft through XSS?
evaluation_notes: Strong: compares all three on XSS and CSRF exposure and lifetime, recommends in-memory access token plus HttpOnly refresh cookie with SameSite/Secure, and stresses XSS prevention. Average: knows localStorage is vulnerable to XSS and HttpOnly helps, but misses the CSRF side. Weak: picks one option with no security reasoning.

question: Users log in successfully, but after about 15 minutes every API call returns 401 and the dashboard just shows empty tables. They are not sent back to the login page. What is happening, and how would you fix it?
model_answer: The JWT access token has expired: its exp claim is 15 minutes after login, so the Spring Security filter rejects it with 401 Unauthorized. The frontend does not treat 401 specially: components catch or ignore the error and render empty data, so the user never learns the session ended. Fix it centrally in an Axios response interceptor: on a 401, call a refresh endpoint (POST /api/auth/refresh, with the refresh token in an HttpOnly cookie) to get a new access token, then retry the original request once. If the refresh also fails, clear the auth state and redirect to /login with a 'session expired' message. Mark retried requests (for example config._retry = true) to avoid an infinite loop, and share one in-flight refresh promise so many parallel 401s trigger only one refresh call.
keywords: expired, exp claim, 401 Unauthorized, response interceptor, refresh token, retry, redirect to login, infinite loop
expected_answer_points: The access token expired (exp claim) and Spring Security returns 401 | The frontend swallows the 401 and renders empty data | Handle 401 centrally in a response interceptor | Call the refresh endpoint with the refresh token and retry the original request once | If the refresh fails, clear auth state and redirect to login | Guard against retry loops and duplicate parallel refresh calls
common_mistakes: Making the token never expire | Checking for 401 separately in every component | Retrying forever, causing an infinite loop of 401 responses | Thinking 401 means the user lacks permission (that is 403)
follow_up_question: Why should the refresh token live longer than the access token but still be revocable on the server?
evaluation_notes: Strong: identifies token expiry and the missing 401 handling, proposes an interceptor with refresh-and-retry-once, fallback to login, and loop/concurrency guards. Average: identifies expiry and suggests redirecting to login but no refresh flow. Weak: suggests longer or non-expiring tokens, or blames the database.

question: How should user passwords be stored in a Spring Boot + MySQL application, and why is BCrypt preferred over plain text, encryption or a fast hash like MD5?
model_answer: Passwords must be stored as a one-way hash, never as plain text or with reversible encryption, so that a database leak does not reveal them. On registration the backend calls encode() on a BCryptPasswordEncoder bean and stores the result (a 60-character string) in MySQL; on login it calls matches(rawPassword, storedHash). BCrypt adds a random salt to every password, so identical passwords produce different hashes and precomputed rainbow tables are useless. It also has a configurable cost factor that makes each hash deliberately slow, which makes brute-force guessing expensive. MD5 and SHA-256 are designed to be fast, so attackers can test billions of guesses per second. Hashing happens on the server; the password travels from React to the backend over HTTPS.
keywords: one-way hash, BCryptPasswordEncoder, salt, cost factor, matches, rainbow tables, brute-force, HTTPS
expected_answer_points: Store a one-way hash, never plain text or reversible encryption | Use BCryptPasswordEncoder: encode() at registration, matches() at login | BCrypt adds a random salt per password, which defeats rainbow tables | Its cost factor makes hashing slow, so brute-force attacks are expensive | MD5 and SHA-256 are too fast for password storage | Hashing is done on the backend; the password is sent over HTTPS
common_mistakes: Re-encoding the password at login and comparing the strings with equals() | Hashing only in React and storing whatever the browser sends | Using a column that is too short for the hash | Treating encryption and hashing as the same thing
follow_up_question: Why does calling encode() twice on the same password give two different strings, and how does matches() still work?
evaluation_notes: Strong: one-way hash, BCrypt with salt and cost factor, encode/matches usage, why fast hashes fail, hashing on the server over HTTPS. Average: says 'use BCrypt, it is secure' with salt but no cost-factor reasoning. Weak: suggests encryption, MD5, or hashing only in the frontend.

question: What is CORS, and why does a React app on http://localhost:5173 get blocked when it calls a Spring Boot API on http://localhost:8080?
model_answer: CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is a browser mechanism that lets a server declare which other origins may read its responses. Under the same-origin policy, a page can freely read responses only from its own origin, and an origin is the combination of scheme, host and port. http://localhost:5173 and http://localhost:8080 differ in port, so they are different origins. When React calls the API, the browser adds an Origin header, and unless the response carries a matching Access-Control-Allow-Origin header, the browser hides the response from JavaScript and logs a CORS error. It is browser enforced, which is why the same request works from Postman or curl. The fix is to allow the frontend origin in the Spring Boot configuration, or to use a dev-server proxy during development.
keywords: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing, same-origin policy, origin, scheme, host and port, Origin header, Access-Control-Allow-Origin, browser enforced, Postman
expected_answer_points: CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is a browser mechanism for relaxing the same-origin policy | The same-origin policy blocks reading responses from other origins | An origin is scheme + host + port, so different ports mean different origins | The server must return Access-Control-Allow-Origin for the calling origin | The browser enforces it, so Postman and curl are not affected
common_mistakes: Thinking CORS protects the API from attackers or scripts outside the browser | Saying the same host means the same origin even when the ports differ | Adding Access-Control-Allow-Origin to the request in React | Believing a CORS error always means the request never reached the server
follow_up_question: How does a Vite dev-server proxy avoid CORS errors during development?
evaluation_notes: Strong: defines CORS and the same-origin policy, explains origin = scheme + host + port, the Allow-Origin response header and browser enforcement. Average: correct definition but cannot explain why different ports matter. Weak: describes CORS as a server firewall or proposes fixing it in React.

question: What is a CORS preflight request? Which requests from a React app to a Spring Boot API trigger one, and what must the server send back?
model_answer: A preflight is an OPTIONS request that the browser sends automatically before a cross-origin request that is not a 'simple request', to ask whether the real request is allowed. It carries Origin, Access-Control-Request-Method and Access-Control-Request-Headers. In a typical React + Spring Boot app most calls are preflighted: PUT, PATCH and DELETE, a Content-Type of application/json, or an Authorization header all make the request non-simple (simple means GET, HEAD or POST with only safelisted headers and a form or text/plain content type). The server must answer the OPTIONS request with a 2xx status and the Access-Control-Allow-Origin, Access-Control-Allow-Methods and Access-Control-Allow-Headers headers (plus Access-Control-Allow-Credentials when cookies are used). Access-Control-Max-Age lets the browser cache the result. Only if the preflight passes does the browser send the actual request.
keywords: OPTIONS, simple request, Access-Control-Request-Method, Authorization header, application/json, Access-Control-Allow-Methods, Access-Control-Allow-Headers, Access-Control-Max-Age
expected_answer_points: The browser automatically sends an OPTIONS request before non-simple cross-origin requests | Triggered by PUT/PATCH/DELETE, a JSON Content-Type or an Authorization header | It carries Origin, Access-Control-Request-Method and Access-Control-Request-Headers | The server must reply 2xx with Allow-Origin, Allow-Methods and Allow-Headers | Access-Control-Max-Age caches the preflight result | The real request is sent only if the preflight succeeds
common_mistakes: Thinking the developer must write code to send the OPTIONS request | Believing a GET with an Authorization header is still a simple request | Letting Spring Security demand authentication on the OPTIONS request | Assuming preflights also happen for same-origin calls
follow_up_question: Why doesn't the browser include the Authorization header on the preflight request, and what does that mean for your security configuration?
evaluation_notes: Strong: OPTIONS sent automatically, correct triggers (methods, JSON, Authorization), request and response headers, Max-Age caching and that the real call waits for it. Average: knows it is an OPTIONS check but is unclear on triggers or required headers. Weak: cannot describe it or thinks the app must send it manually.

question: Your blog app stores user comments in MySQL and shows them to every visitor. A tester posts and it runs for everyone who opens the page. What is this attack, and how do you prevent it across the stack?
model_answer: This is stored XSS (cross-site scripting): attacker-controlled HTML is saved in the database and executed in other users' browsers, where it can steal tokens from localStorage or act as the victim. In React it happens when the comment is rendered with dangerouslySetInnerHTML or written through innerHTML; normal JSX such as {comment.text} escapes the content and is safe. Fixes: render user content as text; if rich text is really needed, sanitize it with a library such as DOMPurify before rendering, and restrict allowed HTML on the backend as well; validate length and format in Spring Boot; add a Content-Security-Policy header that blocks inline scripts and unknown script sources; keep tokens out of JavaScript-readable storage, for example in HttpOnly cookies, to limit the damage; and allow only http/https URLs in user-supplied links, because javascript: URLs can run code.
keywords: stored XSS, cross-site scripting, dangerouslySetInnerHTML, JSX escaping, DOMPurify, sanitize, Content-Security-Policy, HttpOnly
expected_answer_points: It is stored XSS: a malicious script saved in the database runs in other users' browsers | React escapes text in JSX by default; the risk comes from dangerouslySetInnerHTML or innerHTML | Sanitize any HTML that must be rendered (e.g. DOMPurify) and validate on the server | Add a Content-Security-Policy header to block inline and untrusted scripts | Keep tokens in HttpOnly cookies to limit what XSS can steal | Allow only http/https in user-supplied links
common_mistakes: Thinking React makes XSS impossible | Relying only on filtering in the frontend | Confusing XSS with SQL injection | HTML-escaping data when saving it and then escaping it again on display
follow_up_question: What is the difference between stored, reflected and DOM-based XSS?
evaluation_notes: Strong: names stored XSS, explains how it gets into React (dangerouslySetInnerHTML) and gives layered fixes: sanitization, server validation, CSP and HttpOnly tokens. Average: identifies XSS and suggests sanitizing input but misses React escaping or CSP. Weak: calls it SQL injection or has no concrete fix.

question: Your banking app's Spring Boot backend uses session cookies, and a teammate wants to disable CSRF protection because a tutorial did it. Explain how an attacker could then transfer money from a logged-in user's account, and when disabling CSRF protection would actually be safe.
model_answer: CSRF (cross-site request forgery) abuses the fact that browsers attach cookies automatically. While the user is logged in to bank.com, they open evil.com, which auto-submits a hidden form POST to bank.com/api/transfer; the browser sends the session cookie, so the server sees an authenticated request and performs the transfer. The attacker cannot read the response, but the damage is done. Defences: Spring Security's CSRF protection, enabled by default, requires a secret CSRF token that evil.com cannot know, for example via CookieCsrfTokenRepository.withHttpOnlyFalse(), whose XSRF-TOKEN cookie the React app reads and sends back in an X-XSRF-TOKEN header; SameSite=Lax or Strict cookies; and never changing state with GET requests. If the API authenticates only with a JWT in the Authorization header, the browser never adds that header by itself, so a forged cross-site request has no credentials and CSRF protection can be disabled for that stateless API. If the JWT moves into a cookie, CSRF protection is needed again.
keywords: cross-site request forgery, cookies attached automatically, CSRF token, SameSite, XSRF-TOKEN, Authorization header, stateless, GET requests
expected_answer_points: Browsers attach cookies automatically, even on requests triggered by another site | A malicious page submits a forged request that runs with the victim's session | Spring Security's CSRF token (e.g. XSRF-TOKEN cookie sent back as an X-XSRF-TOKEN header) blocks forged requests | SameSite cookies and never changing state with GET add protection | A JWT in the Authorization header is not sent automatically, so CSRF can be disabled for that stateless API | Moving the JWT into a cookie brings the CSRF risk back
common_mistakes: Confusing CSRF with XSS | Thinking CORS alone prevents CSRF, although a simple form POST is sent without a preflight | Thinking POST-only endpoints cannot be forged (a hidden HTML form can send a POST) | Believing HTTPS prevents CSRF
follow_up_question: What is the difference between SameSite=Strict and SameSite=Lax for a user who clicks a link to your site from an email?
evaluation_notes: Strong: walks through the forged request with automatic cookies, lists CSRF tokens, SameSite and safe GETs, and correctly explains why header-based JWT APIs are not exposed while cookie-based ones are. Average: explains the attack but is vague on defences or on the JWT case. Weak: confuses CSRF with XSS or says CORS or HTTPS solves it.

keywords: SQL injection, string concatenation, parameterized query, PreparedStatement, placeholders, BCrypt, matches(), least privilege
expected_answer_points: User input is concatenated into the SQL string, allowing SQL injection | Input such as ' OR '1'='1 changes the query logic and bypasses the login | Use parameterized queries with ? placeholders (PreparedStatement) or JPA bound parameters | Passwords must not be compared as plain text in SQL; use BCrypt and matches() | Frontend validation is not a defence; the DB account should have least privilege
common_mistakes: Trying to fix it by escaping quotes by hand | Believing JPA makes any query safe, even when strings are concatenated into @Query or native SQL | Relying on React input validation to block injection
follow_up_question: Is a native @Query in Spring Data JPA safe from SQL injection? When is it not?
evaluation_notes: Strong: identifies SQL injection from concatenation, shows a working injection example, rewrites with placeholders, and also flags the plain-text password comparison. Average: names SQL injection and suggests prepared statements without showing the fix. Weak: suggests escaping quotes or frontend validation as the fix.

question: A teammate pushed application.properties containing the MySQL password and the JWT signing secret to a public GitHub repo, and also put a payment gateway secret key in the React .env file. What risks does this create, and how should secrets be handled?
model_answer: Anything pushed to a public repository must be treated as leaked: bots scan GitHub for credentials within minutes, and deleting the file later does not remove it from Git history. With the JWT secret an attacker can forge tokens for any user, including admins, and with the database password they can log in to MySQL if it is reachable. First rotate every leaked secret: new DB password, new JWT secret and new payment key. Then keep secrets out of code: reference environment variables in application.properties, for example spring.datasource.password=${DB_PASSWORD} and jwt.secret=${JWT_SECRET}, set the real values on the server, in the hosting platform's settings or in a secrets manager, and add .env files to .gitignore. React is different: every VITE_ or REACT_APP_ variable the app uses is embedded in the public JavaScript bundle, so the frontend must never hold secret keys; calls that need the payment secret go through the Spring Boot backend.
keywords: rotate, Git history, forge tokens, environment variables, secrets manager, .gitignore, JavaScript bundle, backend proxy
expected_answer_points: Secrets pushed to a public repo are compromised even after deletion, because of Git history | A leaked JWT secret lets attackers forge tokens for any user | Rotate all leaked credentials immediately | Load secrets from environment variables or a secrets manager, not source code; keep .env files in .gitignore | React environment variables are bundled into public JavaScript, so no secrets in the frontend | Calls that need secret keys go through the backend as a proxy
common_mistakes: Thinking a new commit that deletes the file fixes the leak | Believing React .env variables are hidden from users | Considering secrets safe just because the repository is private | Not rotating the leaked keys
follow_up_question: How would you supply different database credentials to the same Spring Boot jar in development and production?
evaluation_notes: Strong: treats the secrets as compromised (Git history), rotates them, explains token forgery, moves secrets to environment variables or a secrets manager and knows React env variables are public. Average: says 'use environment variables' but misses rotation or the React bundle issue. Weak: suggests deleting the file or making the repo private as the whole fix.

question: In your app, the 'Delete user' button is shown only to admins in React. A tester logs in as a normal user, copies their JWT, and deletes a user by calling DELETE /api/admin/users/15 from Postman. What went wrong, and how should roles be enforced across the React, Spring Boot and MySQL layers?
model_answer: This is broken access control at the function level: the role check existed only in the React UI. Hiding a button is a user experience decision, not security, because anyone with a valid token can call the API directly from Postman or curl. Roles must be enforced on the backend for every request. Store roles in MySQL (for example a user_roles table), put them in the JWT at login or load them when the token is validated, and let Spring Security enforce them with requestMatchers("/api/admin/**").hasRole("ADMIN") or @PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')") on the service method. A normal user then receives 403 Forbidden. React still reads the roles to show or hide admin screens, but only for user experience. Never trust a role sent in the request body, and add a test that calls each admin endpoint with a normal user's token and expects 403.
keywords: broken access control, roles, Spring Security, hasRole, @PreAuthorize, 403 Forbidden, JWT, user experience
expected_answer_points: Hiding the button in React is only user experience, not security | The API can be called directly with a valid token | Roles must be enforced on the backend with Spring Security (hasRole or @PreAuthorize) | Roles come from MySQL or the validated JWT, never from the request body | A logged-in user without the role receives 403 Forbidden | Admin endpoints are tested with a normal user's token
common_mistakes: Fixing it only by hiding or disabling more UI elements | Trusting a role or isAdmin flag sent in the request body | Returning 401 instead of 403 for a logged-in user who lacks the role
follow_up_question: If an admin's role is removed in the database, how long can their existing JWT still reach admin endpoints, and how would you handle that?
evaluation_notes: Strong: explains that UI hiding is not security, enforces roles in Spring Security from a trusted source (database or validated JWT), returns 403 and mentions testing. Average: says 'check the role on the backend' without saying how or where the role comes from. Weak: suggests hiding the button better or relying on React checks.

question: What are the steps to build and deploy a React + Spring Boot + MySQL application to a Linux server?
model_answer: 1) Database: install MySQL 8 or use a managed instance, create the database and a dedicated database user with only the privileges the app needs, and apply the schema with migrations such as Flyway. 2) Backend: run mvn clean package (or ./gradlew build) to produce an executable jar, copy it to the server and start it with java -jar app.jar using the prod profile and environment variables for the DB URL, username, password and JWT secret; run it as a systemd service or a Docker container so it restarts automatically. 3) Frontend: set the production API URL, run npm run build to produce static files in dist/ (build/ for Create React App), and copy them to the web server. 4) Put Nginx in front with HTTPS, serving the React files and proxying /api to Spring Boot on port 8080. 5) Test the deployed app end to end and check the logs.
keywords: database user, mvn clean package, executable jar, java -jar, npm run build, static files, environment variables, Nginx
expected_answer_points: Set up MySQL with a database, a dedicated user and the schema | Build the backend jar with mvn clean package and run it with java -jar and a prod profile | Supply DB credentials and secrets as environment variables | Build React with npm run build to get static files | Serve the static files and proxy /api through Nginx with HTTPS | Run the backend as a service (systemd or Docker) and verify end to end
common_mistakes: Running npm start (the development server) in production | Using the MySQL root account for the application | Hard-coding localhost URLs that only work on the developer's machine | Leaving spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=create in production, which drops the tables on restart
follow_up_question: How would you package all three parts with Docker Compose?
evaluation_notes: Strong: covers database setup, backend jar build and run with environment variables, React production build, Nginx with HTTPS and running as a service. Average: knows the build commands but misses configuration or how the pieces connect. Weak: runs dev servers in production or cannot describe the build outputs.

question: How do you configure different API URLs and database settings for development and production in a React (Vite) + Spring Boot app? Explain how environment variables behave differently on each side.
model_answer: React with Vite: create .env.development and .env.production with variables prefixed VITE_, for example VITE_API_URL=http://localhost:8080/api and VITE_API_URL=/api, and read them with import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL (Create React App uses REACT_APP_ and process.env). These values are replaced at build time inside the static bundle, so changing one needs a rebuild, and they end up in a public bundle, so they must never contain secrets. Spring Boot reads configuration at runtime. Use Spring profiles (application-dev.properties and application-prod.properties, activated with SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod) and placeholders such as spring.datasource.url=${DB_URL}. Relaxed binding also maps environment variables such as SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD to spring.datasource.password automatically. The same jar therefore runs in every environment by changing only the environment, and secrets are set on the server instead of being committed.
keywords: VITE_ prefix, import.meta.env, build time, runtime, Spring profiles, SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE, relaxed binding, public bundle
expected_answer_points: Vite reads VITE_-prefixed variables through import.meta.env from .env.[mode] files | React variables are fixed at build time and are public, so no secrets | Spring Boot reads configuration at runtime | Use Spring profiles (dev/prod) activated with SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE | Use ${...} placeholders or relaxed binding (SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL) for environment variables | The same jar runs in every environment; secrets are set on the server
common_mistakes: Expecting a changed React .env value to apply without rebuilding | Using process.env.REACT_APP_ variables in a Vite project | Committing production passwords in application-prod.properties | Forgetting the VITE_ prefix, so the variable is undefined
follow_up_question: If you need to change the API URL of an already-built React app without rebuilding it, how could you do that?
evaluation_notes: Strong: explains VITE_ variables and import.meta.env, build-time vs runtime behaviour, public bundle, Spring profiles, placeholders and relaxed binding. Average: knows .env files and profiles but not the build-time vs runtime difference. Weak: hard-codes URLs per environment or puts secrets in React variables.

question: In production you want users to open https://app.example.com for the React UI, send API calls to Spring Boot, and keep MySQL unreachable from the internet. Design this setup using a reverse proxy and explain what the proxy solves.
keywords: reverse proxy, Nginx, TLS termination, proxy_pass, same origin, try_files, firewall, load balancing
expected_answer_points: Nginx is the single public entry point on 443 and redirects HTTP to HTTPS | It terminates TLS and serves the React build as static files | /api requests are forwarded with proxy_pass to Spring Boot on localhost:8080 | The UI and API share one origin, so CORS is not needed in production | Spring Boot and MySQL are not exposed; the firewall opens only 80/443 | try_files falls back to index.html for client-side routes; forwarded headers keep the scheme and client IP
common_mistakes: Exposing ports 8080 and 3306 to the internet | Forgetting the SPA fallback, so deep links return 404 | Not forwarding X-Forwarded-Proto, which causes wrong redirect URLs | Thinking the reverse proxy replaces authentication in Spring Boot
follow_up_question: How would you change this setup to run two Spring Boot instances behind the same Nginx?
evaluation_notes: Strong: clear topology with only Nginx public, TLS termination, static files plus /api proxy_pass, same-origin benefit, SPA fallback and forwarded headers. Average: correct idea of Nginx forwarding /api but misses TLS, network exposure or same-origin benefit. Weak: exposes every service directly or cannot say why a proxy is used.

question: Users complain that the Orders page takes 8 seconds to load in production. How would you find out whether the bottleneck is in React, the network, Spring Boot or MySQL, and what fixes would you expect at each layer?
model_answer: Measure before changing anything. In the browser DevTools Network tab, check each API call: if the calls are fast but the page is still slow, the problem is in React, so use the React DevTools Profiler to find expensive re-renders or huge lists. If a request has a long waiting time (TTFB), the time is spent on the server; if the download is long, the payload is too big. On the backend, log the time per request (or use Spring Boot Actuator metrics) and enable SQL logging to count queries: a classic cause is the JPA N+1 problem, where loading 100 orders fires 100 extra queries for their customers. In MySQL, run EXPLAIN on the slow query to spot full table scans and add an index. Typical fixes: JOIN FETCH or an entity graph and DTO projections for N+1, indexes on filter and join columns, pagination, merging many small API calls into one, compression and caching of rarely changing data, and memoization or list virtualization in React.
keywords: Network tab, TTFB, React Profiler, N+1 problem, EXPLAIN, index, JOIN FETCH, pagination
expected_answer_points: Measure first with the browser Network tab to see which layer is slow | Long waiting time (TTFB) points to the server; fast APIs but slow rendering point to React | Check backend timings and SQL logs to detect N+1 queries | Use EXPLAIN in MySQL and add missing indexes | Fix with JOIN FETCH/DTO projections, pagination and fewer API calls | Optimise React rendering with memoization or list virtualization
common_mistakes: Guessing and adding caching everywhere without measuring | Blaming React without checking the API timings | Fetching every row and filtering in the frontend | Adding an index on every column
follow_up_question: What is the JPA N+1 problem, and how does JOIN FETCH solve it?
evaluation_notes: Strong: measurement-first approach across all layers (Network tab/TTFB, backend timing and SQL logs, EXPLAIN, React profiling) with a matching fix for each. Average: lists plausible fixes but no systematic way to locate the bottleneck. Weak: 'add a faster server' or random caching with no diagnosis.

question: Your React app works on localhost. After deploying the build to Nginx, the home page loads and in-app navigation works, but refreshing the browser on /dashboard or opening a bookmarked /orders/15 gives 404 Not Found. What is the cause, and how do you fix it?
keywords: client-side routing, BrowserRouter, History API, index.html, try_files, fallback, dev server, static files
expected_answer_points: React Router handles routes in the browser with the History API | On refresh the browser asks the server for /dashboard, which does not exist as a file | The dev server falls back to index.html automatically; production Nginx does not | Fix: try_files $uri $uri/ /index.html (or an equivalent rewrite) so React Router handles the path | Keep /api routes separate so the backend still returns real 404s
common_mistakes: Thinking the React routes are broken or must be recreated as Spring Boot endpoints | Redirecting every 404 to the home page, which loses the requested path | Switching to HashRouter without understanding the trade-off | Also sending /api requests to index.html
follow_up_question: If Spring Boot serves the React build from src/main/resources/static, how would you implement the same fallback?
evaluation_notes: Strong: explains client-side routing vs server file lookup, why the dev server hides it, gives the try_files fallback and keeps /api separate. Average: gives the fallback fix without explaining why it happens. Weak: blames React Router configuration or suggests redirecting to the home page.
